blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
There is a real film underneath this book and I want to name it plainly, because the debt is total and because the people in it were real.

Forough Farrokhzad went to a leprosy colony near Tabriz in 1962 and stayed twelve days, at a time when nobody touched those people and nobody looked at them and the official position of the civilised world was that they should be somewhere else. The film she made runs twenty-two minutes. She filmed them eating, praying, playing ball, marrying, having their beards trimmed and their wounds dressed. She filmed a classroom. And she came out with a child, whom she raised.

I first saw it as a teenager in Iran, on a copy of a copy, in a room where we were not supposed to be watching it, and what I felt was not admiration. I was frightened, and underneath the fright, which is harder to write down, I was disgusted. It took me most of my life to understand that this was the film working exactly as she intended, and that I had failed a test she had set on purpose.

This novella is not about her, and the colony in these pages is not the one she filmed, and Homa is not any woman who ever lived. The invention is deliberate and it is the point: real people are owed better than being made into somebody's horror story.
What I have tried to take from her instead is a method.

Her whole body of work runs on one idea, and she stated it more clearly than anybody before or since. Decay is real. Do not deny that it is real. And then look closely enough, and for long enough, and you may find that life is still occurring inside it — children learning, people combing their hair, a wedding, a game, somebody putting on makeup with hands that no longer work.
She never said the house was not black. She said do not look away while it is.

I have spent this book trying to earn that. The village in these pages is a place where terrible things are true and ordinary happiness is also true, at the same time, in the same yard, and neither one cancels the other. I did not want a reader to arrive looking for villains and find them. I wanted a reader to arrive looking for villains and find a wedding.
One more thing, and it is the thing that made the book.

The illness at the centre of this story is not a rotting disease. That is folklore and it is wrong. It kills the nerve, and everything that follows — the ruined hands, the blindness, the shortened fingers — happens because a body stopped sending word and its owner could not be warned. It is a disease of not feeling.

Which means that the people we cannot bear to look at have, in one specific sense, less of a problem than we do. They are not interrupted. And every value I hold, and every value the world outside that wall claims to hold — look at what is in front of you, finish your own thought, stay in the room with somebody who is dying — costs a nerve that none of us can afford to give up.

That is not an argument I agree with. It is an argument I could not answer, and so I have given it to a woman called Ozra and let her make it, and I have not put anybody in the book who can defeat her.

PART ONE — THE CAPTIVE
THE WATER TANK
God, I have a question and it is not the one You are expecting.
I do not want to know why they are ill.
I want to know why the road stops
eleven kilometres short of them
and who decided that,
and whether You were consulted,
and whether You objected.
The road was good for eleven kilometres and then it was not a road.

I remember being angry about that before I was anything else. Not frightened, not sorry — angry, in the specific way of a woman who has spent two days on trains and a morning in a cart and is being told by the surface under her that the last part of the journey is not considered worth the money. The metalling simply ended, mid-slope, without a barrier or a sign, the way a man stops talking when he has decided he has said enough.
After that it was graded dirt, and then track, and then two pale lines in the scrub.

The carter would not go the last half-mile. He put my case down in the road and would not take it further and would not look at me while he explained, and the explanation took some time and included his mother.
So I walked, and I came over the rise at four in the afternoon in September of 1938, and I saw the place I had chosen, from above, all at once.
There was no wall.

I want that recorded at the front of everything, because of what came after and because of what everybody outside believes. Nobody built a wall around us. In September of 1938 there was a shallow bowl of ground with a stream running through it, a line of poplars somebody had planted for the shade, an old brick water tank from the days when the road went somewhere, and thirty-one low houses with nothing at all between them and the world.
Forty-one people. I counted them within the week because I count things; it is the only discipline I have ever kept.

Nobody was waiting for me. That threw me more than a delegation would have. I had prepared myself to be received with gratitude and prepared myself to be received with suspicion, and had a short speech ready for each, and what I got was a hot empty yard, a dog that did not get up, and the sound of somebody sweeping out of sight.
I stood in it for four minutes with my case.
Then a woman came round the corner of the kitchen carrying a basin against her hip and stopped when she saw me, and looked at me for slightly too long, and said:
‘Che khabar?’ [che kha-BAR]
What news. The most ordinary greeting in the language. You say it to a neighbour. You say it to a man selling melons.

I said something polite and stupid — that my name was Homa, that I had come from Tabriz, that I had written ahead, that I was the teacher — and she listened to all of it with an expression I could not read at the time and can read perfectly now, and then she set the basin down with two hands, carefully, flat, releasing it as a separate action from the placing.
‘No,’ she said. ‘Che khabar. What news. From you. Today.’
‘I do not understand.’
‘You will,’ she said, and picked the basin back up, and went in.
I did not understand for eleven days. When I did understand it I had to go out past the poplars and sit down in the dirt.

Because what she had asked me — what everybody in that place asked everybody else, a hundred times a day, laughing, as a greeting — was whether anything had been reported to me. Whether any part of me had sent word. Whether the body I was walking around in had troubled itself, in the past twenty-four hours, to mention anything at all.
And the answer, which I heard four hundred times before I knew what it meant, is: hich khabari nist.
No news.
THE REGISTER
Did You give her the handwriting, God,
or did she teach herself?
Because it is very small and very upright
and it does not vary,
and I have watched her write the names of the dead in it
with the same care she uses for the living,
and I would like to know
which of You is the accountant.
Ozra was twenty-six, which was my age, and this was the first thing anybody told me about her and the way they told it made it a warning.

She had come in the spring. She was already ill — not visibly, not then, but she had the flatness in the left hand that everybody there could read at a glance and that took me a year to see — and she had arrived with a bag, a Qur’an she did not appear to open, and an exercise book.
The exercise book is the thing.

She had begun it before she arrived. On the first page, in a hand so small and upright and regular that it looked printed, she had written the name of every person in that place, and the date they came, and the date somebody first looked at them properly.

Nobody had asked her to. There was no administration. There was a physician who came from the town when he could and a man in Tabriz who signed things, and beyond that we were a collection of people in a bowl of ground with no more organisation than a flock has.
I asked her, in my second week, why she was keeping it.
‘Because nobody else is,’ she said.
‘Someone in the town —’
‘There is a card in an office with a number on it.’ She did not look up. ‘The number is how many. It is not who.’

I said that was a distinction without much practical consequence, or something equally clever, because I was twenty-six and had been a teacher in a city and had a great many opinions I had not yet been charged for.
Ozra put the pen down.

‘My father is in the ground behind the kitchen,’ she said. ‘There is no stone because there was no mason that year. If you go and look you will not find him. In eleven years nobody living will know which part of that ground he is in, and in forty nobody will know he was here at all, and the card in the office will say the number went down by one.’
She picked the pen up again.
‘This is not a distinction,’ she said. ‘This is the only argument I have.’
I have thought about that exchange perhaps once a month for twenty-four years.

I have thought about it because she was right and because she was twenty-six and because in the end the exercise book grew columns I could not have imagined that afternoon, and I helped rule them, and I have never once been able to draw a line between the woman who said this is the only argument I have and the woman who did what she did afterwards.
There is no line. That is what I have concluded. It was the same argument the whole way through.
FEET
They are sitting in the open at sundown
holding each other’s bare feet.
Men and women who are not married.
In front of the children.
Tell me the ruling, God.
Tell me quickly, before I say something,
because I have already opened my mouth once today
and been wrong.

On my third evening the bell went and everybody came out of their houses and sat down in pairs and took off their shoes, and I stood in the middle of the main path with my hands at my sides and thought: I have made a very serious mistake.
I need to set down what I actually saw, in the order I saw it, without the twenty-four years.

I saw a man of about fifty sitting on a low wall with a woman of about thirty in front of him on the step below, and she had her feet up in his lap, bare, and he was holding one of them in both hands with his face four inches from it.
I saw a boy of fourteen doing the same for a widow whose name I did not yet know.

I saw a young married couple who were not paired with each other. He was with an old man. She was with somebody’s grandmother. Neither of them appeared to find this remarkable and neither did anybody else.
I saw perhaps forty people in the open air in the last of the light, touching each other’s bodies, and talking the entire time about bread and arithmetic and somebody’s brother in Ardabil.

I was a teacher from a girls’ school in Tabriz. I had spent two years being told by a modern state exactly how a modern woman conducts herself, and eleven years before that being told by a husband, and my whole life before that by everybody else, and the two sets of instructions did not agree about very much but they agreed about this.
I said, out loud, to nobody: ‘This is not decent.’
A woman two paces away, who I later learned was called Golnaz and who was nineteen and had been there since she was eleven, did not look up from the foot she was holding.
‘No,’ she agreed. ‘It is not.’
And went on looking.
They call it negāh [ne-GAAH]. The plainest word in the language for it. A look. A glance. To have a look at. You would use it about a shop window.

The order never changes and I could do it now in my sleep. Feet first, always. Sole, heel, the sides, between each toe, the skin behind the ankle. Then the shoe is turned over and shaken out and a finger is run all the way round the inside seam, because it is not the stone in the shoe that kills a person, it is the stone that has been in the shoe since Tuesday. Then the hands: palm, back, the web between each finger, under every nail. Then the forearms. Then the face, with a small mirror if both of you can still see and with fingertips if one of you cannot.
Then somebody counts blinks. I thought for a month that this was a children’s game.
Twenty-five minutes, every evening of every year, and the talk goes on the whole way through, and it has exactly the tone of a family shelling beans on a step.

I did not sit down that evening. I stood at the edge of it like an inspector and I went to bed furious, and I lay in the dark composing letters to a ministry, and I fell asleep before I finished the second one.
THE GLASS
I have been given tea, God,
by a smiling woman,
in a room where every single person
was watching me and pretending not to.
You saw what I did.
I would like it struck from the record.
I would like, in general,
a great deal struck from the record.
On the sixth day somebody gave me a glass of tea.
I have to be careful here because I have told this story badly for twenty years, always as a joke against myself, and the joke has worn smooth in the way jokes do and has stopped being true.
Here is what actually happened.

There were six or seven of us in the kitchen in the late morning and the samovar was going and a woman called Sakineh poured for everybody and handed the glasses round, and there was talk, and it was pleasant, and it was the first hour since I had arrived in which I had felt anything other than an intruder.
She handed me mine and I took it and it was too hot.

Not warm. Not hot. The glass was fresh from the tap of a samovar that had been going since dawn and I took it in my fingers the way you take a glass of tea from a woman who is smiling at you, and my hand opened by itself and I made a noise and the glass went on the floor.
Nobody moved.

That is the part that took me years to be able to think about. It was not that they laughed. They did not laugh. The room went on exactly as it had been, the talk continued, somebody got a cloth — and every single person in that kitchen had been watching me from the moment the glass left Sakineh’s hand, and I could feel it, and there was not one face in the room that showed it.
Then Sakineh said, with no edge in it at all: ‘Sorry. It was too hot.’
And there was a pause of perhaps one second.

And then the room laughed — all of it, at once, warmly, at her, at me, at the situation — and somebody thumped the table, and the boy who had gone for the cloth started laughing so hard he had to sit down, and Sakineh said something in Azeri that I did not have, and the whole thing lasted maybe fifteen seconds and then the talk went back to bread.

I understood by the second week that it was done to everybody, that it had been done to every person in that compound at some point in their first month, and that it was the closest thing they had to a ceremony of arrival. If you flinch, you are still outside. If you do not flinch, somebody tells you what they have just done to you, and you laugh, and you are in.
I flinched.
Golnaz told me afterwards, kindly, in the doorway of the bathhouse, that it did not mean anything.
‘Everybody flinches,’ she said. ‘We were all outside once.’
I said: ‘Was I meant to pass?’

And she looked at me with a directness I was not ready for and said: ‘Khanum, you cannot pass. You are going to hold that glass for the rest of your life and it is going to be too hot every single time. We are not being cruel. We only wanted to see it.’
‘See what?’
‘It,’ she said, and did an impression.

It lasted less than two seconds. She snatched an imaginary thing off an imaginary fire, and yelped, and shook her hand out, and hopped once, and did it all with a stupid open animal face — and it was the funniest and most unkind thing I had ever seen in my life, and it was me, and it was everybody I had ever known, and she was nineteen years old.
I did not laugh.
I went and sat behind the water tank for an hour.
WHAT I LEFT
I taught forty girls to read, God.
The state paid me to do it
and my grandmother would not have believed it
and I was proud, and I was right to be proud.
So explain to me
why I am the one who ran,
and why the running felt like the first honest thing
I had done in two years.

I should say what I came from, because otherwise none of what follows makes sense and because I have spent a great deal of the last twenty-four years being asked and giving an answer that is true and is not the answer.
The answer I gave was: I was a teacher and there was a post here and nobody else wanted it.
Both halves are true.
Here is the rest of it.

I was born in 1912, which means I was a child during the years when the country was not really a country — when it was a set of provinces with foreign soldiers walking through them and a famine that took a great many people whose names are also in nobody’s exercise book. I do not remember the politics. I remember being hungry in a way that has never entirely left me and I remember my mother selling a copper tray.
And then there was a man in Tehran who decided that this would stop.

I want to be honest about him because it has become fashionable to be otherwise. He built roads where there had been tracks. He built a railway the length of the country, which people said could not be done and which was done. He took the courts away from the clergy and gave them to men with law degrees. He made an army out of what had been a series of arrangements. He decided the country would be a country and by main force it became one.
And he built girls’ schools.

I taught in one. I was paid by the state to stand in front of forty girls in Tabriz and teach them to read, and my grandmother — who was alive, and who came once and sat at the back and cried — could not have told you a single thing about her own country’s government but knew exactly what it had cost women like her to be unable to read a paper.
I loved it. I want that written down before everything else. I loved my work and I believed in the man who made it possible and I would have argued for him in any room in that city.
Everything he did, he did by decree, and everything he did by decree, he did with police.

I knew that at the time. I want to be exact. I did not learn it afterwards and I did not have it explained to me by history. I knew it in 1936. I simply thought — and this is the whole of my crime, and it took me until 1944 to write the sentence down — that the people it was being done to would come round.
I left Tabriz in the summer of 1938.

There was a post at a place outside the town that had not had a teacher and had been asking for two years, and I applied for it, and there was no competition, and the man in the office looked at me for a long moment and asked whether I understood what kind of place it was, and I said yes.
He said: ‘Nobody understands until they are in it.’
He was right, and he did not know why, and neither did I. I thought he meant the disease.
I did not go there for the children.

I went because I could not stay in a city where I was known, and there is only one thing that makes a woman of twenty-six say that, and I am not going to write it here. I will write it later. I have made myself a promise about the order of these pages and the promise is that I do not get to explain myself before I have described them.
NINETEEN IN TWENTY
They tell me I cannot catch it.
Nineteen out of twenty, they say. Born that way.
So I have been given a wall around me
that nobody can see and I did not build
and did not ask for and cannot take off,
and I am the only person here who has one.
Is that mercy, God, or is that the joke?
Dr Sarabi told me in my fourth week, standing outside the clinic with a cigarette, and he told me kindly, as good news.

Nineteen people out of twenty cannot catch this thing. Not through touch, not through a shared glass, not through years of the same rooms. They are born unable to catch it and they go through their lives never knowing, and there is no test that will tell you which you are until either you get it or you do not.
‘You have been here a month,’ he said. ‘You will be here years. If you were going to have it you would have it.’
That is not medically exact and I did not know enough to argue and he was, as it turned out, entirely right.
I said: ‘Then why is anyone afraid of them?’
And Sarabi — who was fifty and tired and did eleven examinations an hour when he came and who I came to be very fond of — said the truest sentence anybody said to me in my first year.
‘Because it takes years to pass and a second to see.’

I have turned that over ever since. The fear has nothing to do with the transmission. The fear is entirely visual. You could put a healthy man in a room with a sick one for a decade and probably nothing would happen; you can put him in a room for four seconds and something happens to him that no argument will undo.
So they built us a bowl of ground eleven kilometres past the end of a road. Not to stop the disease travelling. To stop the looking.
And this is where I have to say the thing that makes the rest of these pages what they are.
I was not sick.

I was never sick. Not in 1938, not in 1947, not now. I have been in that place for twenty-four years and I have held the hands and the feet and the faces of several hundred people who had it and I have slept in their rooms and eaten their bread and washed in their water, and I have a body that has reported to me faithfully, every day, all my life, like an honest servant, and never once stopped.
I am the only person in this account with nothing wrong with her.

That is not a boast. By the end of these pages you will understand that it is closer to a confession, and that everything I did I did from the outside, and that of all the people who made that place what it became, the one who paid nothing for it was me.
PART TWO — THE WALL
A STONE FROM THE TOWN
They threw something at a child, God,
and the child could not feel it land,
and went on playing,
and it was the rest of us who cried.
I would like to know what You call that.
I have three words for it
and none of them are Yours.

The boy’s name was Rasul and he was nine and he had been with us since the spring, and on a Thursday in October of 1938 four boys from the town came up the track and stood on the rise and threw stones.

This was not the first time. I want to be accurate. There had been shouting from that rise perhaps twice a year for as long as anybody could remember, and it had been endured the way you endure weather, and there was even a sort of curriculum about it — the children were told to come in, and they came in, and it stopped.
That Thursday the children did not come in fast enough.
Rasul was hit twice. Once on the shoulder and once on the side of the head above the ear, and the second one opened him, and he did not know.

That is the thing I have never been able to put down. He did not know. He went on doing what he had been doing, which was arguing with a girl about a game, and he had blood coming down the side of his face and into his collar and he was arguing, and when the girl started screaming he thought she was screaming about the argument.
It took a woman running from the kitchen and turning his head with both hands for him to understand that anything had happened to him at all.
The boys on the rise saw the blood and ran.

I do not think they were monsters. I have made myself say that in this account because it is true and because it would be easier not to. They were nine and eleven and they had been told all their lives what we were, and they came up to look at us the way boys go and look at a dead dog, and one of them threw a stone because boys throw stones, and then there was blood and they ran home and I expect at least one of them was sick.
Sarabi came the next week and put four stitches in and said that it was clean and would heal and that the boy had been lucky, and then he stood outside with his cigarette and said the other thing.
‘He did not put his hand up,’ Sarabi said.
‘He did not know it was coming.’

‘No.’ He looked at the rise. ‘Khanum, I have been doing this eleven years. A child who can feel does not stand there. A child who can feel ducks, or runs, or covers his head, and the stone hits his arm. They cannot do any of that. Not because they are slow. Because there is nothing to be quick about.’
I said something about a fence.
And Sarabi said: ‘A fence is for keeping animals off a crop. What you want is a wall.’
It took two weeks for anybody to say it out loud in a room, and when it was said it was said by a woman of sixty called Effat who had never in my hearing offered an opinion on anything.
She said: ‘We should not be able to be seen from the rise.’
That was all. That was the entire argument, and it went round that bowl of ground in an afternoon, and by the end of the week there were men measuring.
I want to set down clearly what happened next because everything that this place became rests on it and because the world outside has it exactly backwards.
*Nobody walled us in.*

There was no ministry, no order, no soldiers, no fence erected around a colony by a frightened administration. There was a nine-year-old boy who bled without knowing it, and a woman of sixty who said we should not be able to be seen, and then two hundred cartloads of mud brick that we made ourselves out of the ground we were standing on, and eleven men and a great many women, and thirty-one months.
We built it. From the inside. Because the outside was worse.

And the state, which in those years was busy curing the country by decree and had a great deal to be getting on with, never noticed and never asked and, so far as I have ever been able to establish, has no record that it exists.
THE MAN IN THE HAT
He came in a hat, God.
A grey European hat with a brim,
and a coat that did not fit him,
and he took the hat off in the yard
and held it in both hands like something he had been made to carry,
and I have never seen a man look so much
like a letter that had been opened by somebody else.
Sheikh Amanollah [a-maan-ol-LAAH] arrived in November of 1938 to bury a woman and stayed nine years.

He came up that track in a grey felt hat and a European overcoat with the shoulders wrong, and he was forty-four and looked sixty, and he had the beard and nothing else, and when he took the hat off in the yard and stood holding it I understood something about the previous ten years of my country that two years of teaching in a state school had not taught me.
I want to explain what had been done to men like him, because I did not know it at the time and because it explains everything he did afterwards.

He had trained eleven years. He had a licence to teach and to judge and he had done both, in a district south of Tabriz, in courts that had settled marriages and inheritance and debt for four hundred years.

Then the courts were taken away and given to men with law degrees from Tehran, which — and I have to be honest in these pages or there is no point writing them — was in many ways a good thing, and I said so at the time, loudly, in a staff room.

Then the endowments were taken under state control. Those endowments were land and rents left by the dead to keep the mosques and the seminaries and the men in them. When the state took the administration of them, a man like Amanollah did not become poor exactly. He became a person waiting for a payment from an office, which is a different thing and does something to you.
Then the seminaries emptied, partly because young men were conscripted and partly because it had been made clear that this was not a career for a young man in a modern country.
Then they licensed the clothes.

I need to be very plain about this because people forget it and because Amanollah never once complained about it in nine years. A man could be required to prove he was entitled to wear the turban and the robe. There was a document. If you did not have the document you wore a hat and a coat like a clerk, and if you wore the robe anyway you could be stopped in the street by police and made to take it off.
So my country, which had built me a school and paid me to teach in it, also required a forty-four-year-old man to carry a piece of paper certifying his right to dress as himself.
He came to bury a woman because there was nobody else who would come.

And afterwards he stood in the yard with his hat in his hands, and Effat brought him tea, and he drank it and looked round the bowl of ground at thirty-one houses and the beginnings of a wall and forty-one people who had no one at all.
And he said: ‘Do you have anyone?’
And Effat said: ‘No. There is a teacher, Homa Khanum, from the town. There is nobody else.’
He put the glass down with two hands, which he had learned in about four minutes, and which nobody had taught him.
‘Then I will come on Thursdays,’ he said.
He came on Thursdays for two months and then he came on Mondays as well and then in February he brought a bag.
I asked him once, years later, why he stayed. He was a truthful man in a way that eventually cost him everything, and he did not give me the answer about God.
He said: ‘Because here I am necessary.’
And then, because he could not help himself: ‘Which is a poor reason, and I have examined it, and it has not improved.’
THE RULE ABOUT FEET
They have made a rule, God,
and they made it out loud, in a yard, in front of everybody,
and they did not consult a book
and they did not consult a man
and they did not consult You.
They consulted a graveyard.
I am told this is how most rules were made
before somebody wrote them down.
The pairing rule was made in the spring of 1939 and it was made because a woman called Zohreh died of a foot.

She was fifty-one. She had gone blind the previous year — not from the disease directly, but in the way that place went blind, which is that the wire to the eyelid dies and you stop closing the eye and you do not know you have stopped, and the eye dries out across months and clouds from the middle, and there is no pain at any point in the process to tell you it is happening.
She lived alone. Her husband was dead. Her sister looked at her when she remembered.

There was an opening in the sole of her left foot that went down and down for something like five weeks, and by the time it was a smell it was in the bone, and Sarabi came and took the leg below the knee on the kitchen table, and she died eleven days later of what he wrote down as fever.
We buried her, and Amanollah did the rites, and afterwards there was the meeting.

It was not a meeting. There was no such thing here. It was thirty or forty people in the yard after a funeral, standing about, and Effat said the thing that Effat says, which is always four words long and always ends the discussion before it starts.
She said: ‘Nobody looked at her.’

And a man said that Zohreh’s sister should have looked at her, and there was some agreement, and then Golnaz — who was twenty by then and had been in that place nine years and had no patience — said the thing that changed how everybody in that bowl of ground lived for the next twenty-three years.

‘Her sister cannot see either,’ she said. ‘Neither of them can see. You have paired the two blind women together because they are sisters and you have been very satisfied about it. That is not a pair. That is two people agreeing to die politely.’
There was a silence of some length.
‘Then who looks at whom?’ somebody said.

And Golnaz said: ‘Whoever can see looks at whoever cannot. That is the only rule. Everything else is how we have always done it, and how we have always done it has just cost us a woman’s leg and then the woman.’
I want to be exact about what that meant, because it is the strangest thing about that place and the thing I have never been able to explain to anybody outside it without watching their face change.

It meant that pairs were no longer husband and wife. It meant they were no longer brother and sister, or mother and daughter, or the arrangements of habit and decency that everybody had been using since the place began.

It meant that a woman of sixty with good eyes was paired with a man of thirty who had none. It meant a boy of fourteen and a widow of fifty. It meant that men and women who were not married to each other and not related to each other would sit down in the open at sundown, every evening, and hold each other’s bare feet in their laps and go over them with their eyes four inches away.
In 1939. In a village in the province of Azerbaijan.

I was twenty-seven and had been in that yard eight months and I did not say a word, because I had already said this is not decent once, in my third evening, and I had been agreed with by a nineteen-year-old who did not look up.
And every face in that yard turned, not to me, and not to Golnaz.
They turned to the man in the hat.

Amanollah stood there with forty people waiting, and he was four months into a place he had come to as a favour, and he was the only person present with the standing to stop it, and he knew that, and everybody knew he knew.
I have thought about what he did for twenty-three years.

He did not rule. That is the point and it is the whole of his character. He did not say it was permitted and he did not say it was forbidden and he did not reach for the books he had left in a house in a district that no longer wanted him.
He said: ‘How many are blind?’
Somebody counted. Nine, at that time, out of sixty-one.
He said: ‘And how many will be?’
And nobody answered, because the answer was everybody, eventually, one way or another.
Amanollah put his hat on.
‘I cannot find the ruling that would prefer her leg,’ he said, and walked back to the shrine.

That was all. He never spoke about it again in nine years, to me or to anyone. He did not experience it as a compromise and he certainly did not experience it as the first crack in anything. He would have told you, and did tell me once, that it was the plainest decision of his life and that any man with the training would have made it.
He was wrong about that. A great many men with the training would have preferred the leg.
BAHMAN’S NAIL
I laughed today, God.
I want to report it in the correct manner.
Word has come from the throat. Dated this afternoon.
There was a man, and a nail, and five weeks,
and I laughed until I had to hold the wall,
and I have been sitting here since
trying to work out what has happened to me.
There is a scoreboard. I had better explain it now because it runs under everything else that happens in these pages and because it is the thing that made me one of them.
Two hundred people — sixty-one, then, but two hundred later — doing the same task every evening for years will compete at it. Of course they will. You would.
What is being competed for is the find.
An opening in a sole. A splinter. A blister that has already burst and dried. A burn nobody reported. A stone in a shoe.

And the scoring is not by size. This is what took me a year to understand and what makes it, in the end, so much worse and so much funnier than it looks. A fresh stone is nothing. Any fool finds a fresh stone; the stone is on top of the foot, the foot is pink, you are done. The scoring is *by age.*
A stone that has been in a shoe since Tuesday is a result.

And the person congratulated is not only the finder. The owner is congratulated too — because it takes a particular kind of man to walk on something for nine days without his partner catching it, and because it reflects extremely badly on the looker, and everybody in the yard knows whose looker it is, and the looker has to sit there while it is held up.
The find is announced. It is held up between finger and thumb. It goes round the pairs, and people examine it, and there is a sort of applause.

And the owner is required to perform astonishment, which is the joke inside the joke, because they genuinely are astonished. They had no idea. It is their own foot and the news is arriving four days late by a route they do not control, and the House has built an entire theatrical register for receiving reports about its own body.
Word has come from the foot, a man will say, holding up a piece of gravel. Dated last Tuesday. Sends regards.

Bahman was thirty-six in 1940 and he was a roofer before, and he was not a funny man. That matters. Bahman had no jokes. He was slow and pleasant and had opinions about mud brick that he would share at length.

On an evening in June of 1940 the woman who looked at him — Effat, of all people — went round the inside seam of his left shoe with a finger, the way you do, and stopped, and did not say anything, and turned the shoe over and shook it, and nothing came out.
Then she got the knife.

It was a nail head. It had come up through the sole from underneath, the way nails do in a roof, and the point had gone into the ball of his foot and turned over, and the wound had closed round it and closed again and there was tissue grown over the whole of it.
Sarabi came the following week and looked and said, without any particular drama, that by the state of the thing it had been there about five weeks.
Five weeks.

And Bahman — who had no jokes, who had never made anybody laugh in his life — looked at the nail head in the palm of Effat’s hand, and looked round at forty people who had all stopped what they were doing, and said, in the flattest voice you ever heard:
‘I have been wondering why I am so bad at roofs now.’
I do not know why that is the funniest thing I have ever heard. I have told it perhaps two hundred times in twenty-three years and it has never once failed and I still cannot take it apart.
I laughed until I could not stand up.
I want to be precise about this because it is the hinge of my life and I have never told anybody, including Golnaz, including Ozra.

I laughed at a man who had walked on a nail for five weeks without knowing. I laughed in a yard full of people who could not feel their own bodies, at the fact that they cannot feel their own bodies, and every single one of them was laughing with me, and I was not laughing at them and I was not laughing with them either.
I was laughing from inside it.

And when it stopped, and everybody went back to their feet, I went and stood behind the kitchen with my hand flat on the wall, because I had understood in the middle of it — in the actual middle of the laugh, while it was still going — that I had crossed something, and that I could not go back over it, and that there was nobody left in Tabriz or anywhere else I could explain this to.
Two years earlier I had stood in that same yard and said this is not decent.
Effat put the nail in a tin. It is still in the tin. It has been brought out at every wedding since 1940 and Bahman is asked to tell it and pretends he would rather not.
Nobody has ever beaten it.
THE WALL IS FINISHED
It is finished, God, and it took thirty-one months,
and we made the bricks out of the ground we were standing on,
and I carried some of them myself.
It is a wall to keep us from being seen.
It is a wall to keep us where we are.
It is the same wall.
You made the world and I would like to know
whether You have ever built anything
that only did one thing.
We finished it in May of 1941 and there was no ceremony, because it did not finish, it simply stopped having gaps.

Half a mile round. Mud brick, made in the yard from the ground under our feet and dried in stacks and carried by everybody who could carry, including me, for thirty-one months. Chest high in most places. Higher on the north side where the rise is.
It is not a fortification. A man could get over it with a hand and a knee. A determined boy could get over it in four seconds and one did, in 1943, and was fed.
It was never built to stop anybody coming in.

It was built so that we could not be seen from the rise, exactly as Effat said in a yard on an afternoon in 1938, and it did that, completely, from the day it closed. Nobody has thrown a stone at this place in twenty-one years.
And here is what else it did, and I have never been able to decide the order to put these in.

Inside a wall, a place becomes a place. That sounds like nothing. It is not nothing. Before the wall we were a set of houses that people had been sent to. Within a year of the wall we were somewhere, with an inside and an outside and a way that things were done in here, and the way things were done in here began to differ from the way things were done out there — and once that has started it does not stop, and nobody chooses it, and nobody notices it happening.
And a wall does something to the people inside it that I did not expect and have never seen written down anywhere. It makes leaving into an event.

Before the wall a person could drift out. Three did, in my first year, and nobody remarked on it. After the wall, going out meant going through the gate, and the gate is in one place, and there are always four people in the yard, and so every departure became a thing that was witnessed.
Nobody stopped anybody. Nobody ever stopped anybody, in twenty-four years. The gate has never been locked and there is a chain on the inside for the wind and that is all.
Eleven people have gone out in twenty-four years.
The rounding was mine. I will take that one and I have never been sure whether to be proud of it.

It was the autumn of 1941 and I was watching a man called Yunes carry a basin past the corner of the school and catch his hip on the brick, and it opened him, and he did not know until the evening. And I stood there and thought about the fact that we had spent thirty-one months building a wall to stop stones coming in from a rise, and had then filled the inside of it with four hundred corners.
I got a rasp from the carpenter.
I did the school doorway first, on my own, over about three evenings, and it took much longer than I expected and my hands blistered and I was extremely pleased with myself.

Then Golnaz did the kitchen. Then two of the boys did the water channel, badly, and then did it again properly. And it went round that place the way things went round that place, without a meeting, and it never stopped, and by the middle of the fifties there was not one right angle at the height of a hip anywhere inside that wall. Every doorframe. Every table. Every kerb. The lips of the stone channel worked round by hand, over years, so that the whole watercourse has the soft shoulders of something in a bathhouse.
I have watched a woman spend an afternoon rasping the edge of a step for a man who died the following spring.
That is what we did instead of medicine.
WHAT SARABI SAID
He said it kindly, God.
He said it standing outside the clinic with a cigarette
and he did not know what he had said
and I did not know what I had heard
and it took six years to come round to us.
Do You count a sentence as an act?
I am asking because I would like to know
how many I am carrying.
Sarabi came in the October of 1941, a month after the country stopped being what it had been, and he was in a foul mood and he had no supplies and he did eleven examinations an hour for two days.
I made him tea and we stood outside the clinic in the cold, and he smoked, and he talked to me the way a tired man talks to the only other educated person within eleven kilometres.

He said the war had taken his morphine. He said there were British lorries on the Tabriz road and Russian ones north of it and that he had been stopped twice in a week by boys with rifles who could not read his papers. He said a man in the ministry had told him that the country was being administered.
Then he said: ‘There is a drug.’
I did not know what he meant.

He said there was work coming out of America, that there had been trials, that there was something — he called it by a name I did not write down and could not have spelled — that appeared to actually stop this thing. Not manage it. Stop it. He said within ten years, maybe five, it would be a matter of taking something by mouth for a period of years and then not having it any more.
I said that was the best news I had ever heard.
And Sarabi — who was fifty-three and decent and exhausted and who was not thinking about what he was saying, and who I have never blamed and who died in 1946 of something ordinary — said:
‘Yes. And then what happens to this place?’
I said I did not follow.
‘Khanum.’ He put the cigarette out on the wall. ‘Look at it. Sixty-one people. A school. A kitchen. A wall you built yourselves. What is it that holds all of that together?’
‘I do not know. People. Habit.’

‘No,’ he said. ‘It is the disease. It is the only thing every person here has in common and it is the only reason the state leaves you alone and it is the only reason any of you is here rather than somewhere else.’ He was not being cruel. He was talking out loud on a cold night. ‘Cure them and there is no reason for this. There is a bowl of ground eleven kilometres past the end of a road with sixty-one people in it who have nowhere to go and no work and hands that no one will hire and no family that will have them back. They will not be a village. They will be sixty-one cured beggars, dispersed, and in twenty years nobody will remember that any of this was here.’
I said: ‘Then they will be cured beggars instead of sick ones.’
And he said: ‘Yes,’ and looked at the wall for a while, and said: ‘I only mean that it is a strange thing to be able to see coming and not know whether to want it.’
Then he got into the car and went back to the town.
He said it once. He never said it again and I am satisfied he never thought about it twice, and he was dead before any of it happened.
I did not repeat it. I want that on the record too, for whatever it is worth, which is nothing.
I did not repeat it, and it stayed in me for six years like a stone in a shoe, and I did not know it was there, and by the time anybody found it there was tissue grown over the whole of it.
PART THREE — REBELLION
THE SHAH ON A BOAT
Sixteen years, God.
Roads, a railway, a school with my name on the register,
and it ended in nine days
because two armies decided it should,
and there was nothing anybody could do,
and I stood in a yard eleven kilometres past the end of a road
and understood that I had believed in something
the way a child believes in a father.
In August of 1941 the British came up from the south and the Russians came down from the north and in nine days it was over.

I do not have a good account of it. Nobody in that bowl of ground did. We heard it in pieces over about three weeks, from a carter, from Sarabi, from a boy who had been to the town for flour and came back with a story that turned out to be half right, which was better than most.

The army that had taken sixteen years to build did not fight. That is the part that people in the towns could not say out loud for a long time afterwards. Units were told to stand down and they stood down and some of them simply walked home in whatever they were wearing.

And the man who had done all of it — the roads, the railway, the courts, my school, the hat on Amanollah’s head — was put on a boat by foreigners and sent to an island in Africa, and his son, who was twenty-one and whom nobody had heard of, was told he was now the king.
I sat on the step of the school and did not go in for a whole morning.
I want to try to describe what that was, because I have never been able to and because it is not patriotism and it is not grief and it does not have a word.

I had ordered my entire adult life around a project. I had defended it in staff rooms. I had used its language — progress, the modern woman, the backward elements — and I had used that language about actual people I knew by name. I had believed that the country was being made well, by force, quickly, and that the force was regrettable and the speed was necessary and that in twenty years nobody would be able to remember why anybody had objected.
And it was gone in nine days, and everything it had broken stayed broken.
That is the sentence. It took me three years to be able to write it down and I still cannot read it without wanting to put my hand over it.

Everything it had broken stayed broken. The tribes it moved did not go back. The men it put in prison did not come out into a world that made sense to them. Amanollah did not get his robe back — nobody ever gave it back, there was no ceremony of restoration, the licence simply stopped mattering and he went on wearing the hat for another two years out of what I can only call habit and possibly spite. The women it uncovered in the street did not have those years returned to them.
The cure stopped and the surgery stayed.
I was twenty-nine years old and I had been, in a small and entirely sincere way, one of the surgeons.
THE CONSIGNMENT
There is no flour, God, and there is no kerosene,
and the man who used to bring them says
that it is not his fault and he is right.
I am not asking for bread.
I am asking who I should be angry at,
because I have got quite a lot of it now
and it has nowhere to go
and it is beginning to go inward.
Occupation is not what people who have not had one imagine.

There were no atrocities on that road. I want that plain. In four years I saw perhaps thirty foreign soldiers in total and every one of them was bored and most of them were younger than my pupils and two of them gave a boy chocolate.
What occupation is, is that everything is being taken somewhere else, for somebody else’s war, and nobody is in charge of the taking.

The grain went north. There were requisitions and there were purchases at prices set by people who were not selling and there was a great deal that simply moved because moving it was easier than explaining why it had not moved. The trains that the old Shah had built to hold the country together were now the most efficient machine for emptying it, running day and night with other people’s cargo.
And the price of flour in Tabriz went up by a factor I was told and did not believe and later believed.

Our consignment came monthly. Flour, kerosene, a little tea, and a small quantity of the ointments and dressings that were all anybody had for us. It came on a cart from the town under an arrangement that predated everybody and that nobody could produce a document for.
In the winter of 1941 it came three weeks late.
In the spring of 1942 it did not come at all in March, and came in April at two-thirds, and in May it came at half and the man who brought it would not get down off the cart.
Effat asked him what had happened.
He said: ‘Everything.’
And that was, in fact, the whole answer, and we did not ask him again in four years.
Here is what happens in a place like ours when the flour halves.

Nothing dramatic. Nobody riots. What happens is that people who are already carrying something begin to carry it less well. A man who was managing his feet stops managing his feet, because he is tired and because the evening is when he would have been looked at and he has gone to lie down instead. A woman who was blinking twenty times a minute with somebody reminding her blinks eleven times a minute because the woman who was reminding her is queueing.

The disease did not get worse. The disease is not sensitive to politics. The disease went on doing the one thing it does, which is to take away the warnings, and we went on doing the one thing we could, which is to warn each other, and we got worse at it, because we were hungry.
That is how the winter of 1942 was made. Not by the illness. By arithmetic in an office two provinces away.
THE OFFICER AT THE GATE
A man came to help us today, God,
and we lied to him,
and we lied to him beautifully,
all of us, at once, without a word of arrangement,
and afterwards nobody mentioned it.
I did not know we could do that.
I would like to know when we learned,
and I would like to know
what else we can do that I have not seen yet.
He came in the autumn of 1942 and he came alone, which should have told us he was nobody, and he had a bicycle and a satchel and a clipboard.
He was perhaps thirty-five. His shoes were wrong for that track and he had walked the last half-mile pushing the bicycle. He had a cold. I remember that because he apologised for it twice.

He was from the provincial administration and he had a list of settlements and he was doing an entitlement census for the ration. That was all. There was a scheme by which places with a registered population received an allocation, and we had never been on it, because nobody had ever counted us, because we did not exist in the sense that mattered.
He had found us on an old map. He said that. He said, cheerfully, that we were the only thing on his list all week that had turned out to be real.
He wanted a number.
And what happened over the next forty minutes is the single most frightening thing I saw in that place before the vote, and it was frightening precisely because it was so pleasant.

Effat gave him tea. He sat on the low wall by the kitchen with his clipboard on his knees and his cold, and people came and went, and there was a great deal of good humour about the bicycle, and the boys were shooed and came back.
And he asked how many people lived here.
And Effat said: ‘Twenty-two.’
There were ninety-four of us.

I was standing four feet away with a basin in my hands and I did not move and I did not make a sound, and I want to be honest about what was in my head, which was not loyalty and was not calculation. It was simply that I did not know what the true number was supposed to be. I had not been told a number. Nobody had told me anything.
Then Golnaz, who was twenty-three, said: ‘Twenty-two now. There were more.’
And Ozra, from the doorway of the school, said: ‘Twenty-six last spring.’

And the man wrote it down and asked, decently, whether the ones who had gone had gone to the town, and a woman I barely knew said no, and looked at the ground, and he understood her to mean they had died, and stopped asking, and apologised.

Nine or ten people spoke in those forty minutes. Every single one of them said something consistent with twenty-two. Nobody contradicted anybody. Nobody hesitated. A man mentioned a family that does not exist, in the past tense, and two people made small sad noises of agreement, and the man from the administration made a note.

He got his entitlement schedule out and calculated our ration on twenty-two persons and said, sincerely, that it was not much but that it was better than nothing, and that he was sorry it had taken so long, and that we should have been on this list years ago.
Then he pushed his bicycle back up the track.
We got a ration for twenty-two people for the rest of the war, which was slightly less than the arrangement we already had, and it was on paper, and it came.
I found Ozra in the school afterwards and I was shaking, and I said: what was that.
And she said: ‘He was going to write a number in a book.’
‘Yes.’

‘Ninety-four is a village,’ she said. ‘Twenty-two is a remnant. A village on a list in a provincial office is a thing an official will eventually want to visit, or move, or improve. A remnant is a rounding error.’ She closed the exercise book. ‘Nobody has ever done anything to us that started with somebody being interested.’
I said: ‘Who decided?’
And this is the answer I have carried for twenty years.
She said: ‘Nobody decided. Effat said twenty-two.’
TYPHUS
They are dying in the town, God.
Not of ours. Of the ordinary thing that comes
when the flour halves and the water is bad
and too many people are sleeping in one room.
The road is closed.
We are the safest place in the province
and it is because nobody will come near us,
and I do not know whether to laugh
and I am learning that here that is not a real question.
In the winter of 1942 there was typhus in Tabriz and along the road, and it was bad, and it did what that disease does in a bad year in a hungry city, which does not need describing.
The road was closed for eleven weeks.
Our wall, which we had built to stop stones, kept out an epidemic that would have gone through ninety-four undernourished people in a bowl of ground like fire through a stack.
Nobody came. Nobody came for eleven weeks, and no cart, and no doctor, and no ration, and no news except what a boy shouted from the rise once, which was not accurate.
And we sat in there through the coldest weeks of that decade with what we had.

Which was: no flour after the first month, and then flour of a kind, and then whatever the kitchen could do with what was in the store, which by February was barley and dried mulberry and an amount of rice that Effat measured in a cup she kept in her apron.
There were no jokes in the kitchen after January. I noticed it and could not think about it.

I have written a great deal in these pages about how funny that place was and I have meant every word. It was the funniest place I have ever lived and I have never laughed since 1947 the way I laughed between 1940 and 1946.

And it goes. That is the thing nobody tells you about a place like that. It goes when there is nothing left to convert. The whole apparatus — the news from the foot, the scoreboard, the impressions, the terrible cheerful questions at weddings — all of that is a machine for turning something unbearable into something that can be carried across a room. It needs a certain amount of slack to run on. Below a certain point there is no slack, and the machine stops, and what is left is simply what is actually happening, which is what the machine was built to prevent you from looking at directly.
By the middle of February the evening Looking was being done in near silence.
Ninety-four people, in pairs, on the walls, in the cold, going over each other’s feet with their eyes four inches away, and nobody saying anything at all.
I have never seen anything more like prayer and I have never been able to say so to Amanollah.
ELEVEN
They died between the eleventh of February and the nineteenth of March, 1943.
Golnaz’s mother, Sakineh, who had given me the tea. She was fifty-eight. A chest thing, four days.
Yunes, who had opened his hip on the corner of the school in 1941 and made me get the rasp. Fifty-one. His foot, and then his blood.
A woman called Robab, sixty-six, in her sleep, and we did not find her until the evening because her pair was also unwell and did not come out, and I will not write more about that.
Two boys, brothers, aged nine and eleven, four days apart, of something that came in with the flour in January and that Sarabi later said was probably not typhus and could not tell me what it was.

Effat’s husband Hasan, who was seventy-one and who had been failing for two years and whom nobody was surprised about, and whose death was still not a mercy, and I will not have it written down that it was.
A man called Nader, thirty-nine, who fell.

Zohreh’s sister, who was blind, and who I have not named in these pages and will not, and who had been paired properly since 1939 and was found anyway, and whose feet were the thing, and whose pair was one of the boys.

A woman of twenty-eight, Simin, and her child, born in the second week of March and dead in the third, and Simin four days after, and there is no more to say about that and I have started this sentence six times.
Eleven, in five weeks, out of ninety-four.

We buried them in the ground behind the kitchen because the ground behind the kitchen is where we bury people, and it was frozen for the first three and we did what you do, and Amanollah did the rites for every single one of them.
He did the full rites. Not the short form. The full washing and the full prayer, eleven times in five weeks, at his age, in that cold, with his hands.
I helped with four of the women because there was nobody else.

I had never done it. I was thirty-one years old and I had been raised in a city by people who paid other people to do this. Effat showed me, on Sakineh, on the second day, and she showed me the way she said everything, which was in four words and without looking at me.
She said: ‘Warm the water first.’

That is the sentence I have thought about most in my life. Not any of the poetry. Not anything said to me by a man or by my mother or by the state. Warm the water first — for a woman who cannot feel it, who is dead, who will never know, from a woman with no fingers left on her right hand, in a February with no kerosene.
There is no argument in that. There is nothing to agree or disagree with.

Everything I did afterwards, everything in the second half of this account that people will find difficult, comes out of a kitchen in February 1943 and a basin of water that somebody insisted on warming.
THE RITES
He is standing over the eleventh one, God,
and he is saying the words,
and I have watched him say them
over a boy of nine and over a woman with her child,
and I am going to ask this once and then not again.
Was he speaking to You?
Because he has stopped believing that he was,
and he has not stopped speaking,
and I want to know which of those two things You noticed.

The nineteenth of March, and the eleventh grave, and Nader had fallen off a roof he had no business being on and had broken something inside himself that Sarabi could not have fixed if Sarabi had been there.
It was cold and it was the end of it and everybody knew it was the end of it because the road had opened four days earlier.
Amanollah did the rites.

And afterwards, when the others had gone in, he stood at the edge of that ground with his hands at his sides, and I was fifteen feet away with the basins because somebody had to carry the basins, and he said — not to me, and not loudly, and not in the voice a man uses when he wants to be overheard:
‘I have said it eleven times.’
I did not answer. I have been grateful ever since that I did not answer.

He said: ‘I have said it correctly eleven times. I have not left out a word. I have said it over a child of nine and I have said it over a woman who was in labour eleven days ago and I have not left out a single word, and I have listened, and there is nothing there.’
Then he said: ‘I do not mean that He is cruel. Cruel would be something. Cruel would be a party to it.’
And then he stood there for a while.
I want to put down exactly what he did next because I have thought about it more than anything else in my life and because everything he did in 1947 comes out of it.
He picked up his hat.
He put it on.
And he said: ‘Thursday I will do the forty-day for Sakineh. Her daughter will want it done properly and it will comfort her and I will do it properly.’
That is the whole of it. That is what a loss of faith actually looks like in a man of that kind, and it is not a shout and it is not a departure and it is not an argument with anybody.

He did the rites for another four years. He did them exactly, and beautifully, and on time, and he taught two boys to do them after him, and he sat with the dying and said the things you say and held hands he could not feel and comforted people, night after night, for four years, with nothing at the other end of it at all.
I asked him once, in 1945, whether it was dishonest.
And he said: ‘Dishonest to whom?’
I said: ‘To them.’

And Amanollah said: ‘Khanum, I have never in my life told anybody that God answers. That is not in the prayer. The prayer says that we praise Him and that we ask. I have never once said that anything comes back.’ He looked at me. ‘Go and read it. Everybody thinks it is in there. It is not in there. It has never been in there. It is a thing we all agreed to assume, out of politeness, some time before any of us were born.’
I went and read it.
He was right.
PART FOUR — ANOTHER BIRTH
THE FLAT HOUR
I went out to the wall, God,
and I did not come back for most of a day,
and I have to tell somebody
and there is nobody in this bowl of ground I can tell,
so I am telling You,
and I notice that this is the first time in five years
I have asked You for anything
other than an explanation.
I should describe the flat hour first, because it is where all of this happened and because everybody who has ever visited that place has looked directly at it and seen nothing.
Between one and three in the afternoon the House sits down.

It is not a rule. Nobody instituted it. In a hot country people rest in the middle of the day and there is nothing remarkable about it, and if you were standing in that yard at one o’clock you would say: they are having a rest, as anybody would.
What is different — and it took me four years to see it and I only saw it because I am the one person there who could not do it — is that they do not move.

Put a person on a step and tell them to sit still and time them. Go on. You will get four seconds, or nine, and then something will happen: a hand to the face, the weight shifting, a swallow, a scratch, a knee resettling. That is not restlessness. That is the ordinary condition of being a person. We are being addressed constantly by our own skin and we answer every single time and we have no idea we are doing it.
In that yard I have watched a man of sixty sit on a step for fifty-one seconds and blink four times and do nothing else at all.

I counted, because I am the one who counts things. The shortest I ever recorded was nineteen seconds and the average was a little over thirty, and there was no arrangement about it and no one thought it was interesting and when I asked what they did in the afternoon they said: nothing. We sit. And they meant it, and for four years they were telling the truth.
For four years there was nothing there.

I want that stated plainly because of everything that comes after and because I am the only person alive who can state it. From 1938 to 1942 the flat hour was an hour of people sitting down, and no one saw anything, and no one described anything, and there was no garden and no wall and nobody standing behind anybody.
It was empty. It was just quiet.

Then it was February 1943 and eleven people were in the ground behind the kitchen and I had helped wash four of them, and on the eighteenth of March, the day before Nader’s funeral, I went out to the northern wall in the flat hour and sat down on the ground with my back against the brick because I could not be in a room with anybody.

I was thirty-one. I had not slept properly since January. I had watched a woman of twenty-eight die four days after her child and I had been in the room and I had been useful and afterwards I had gone out and been sick against the side of the school.
And I sat down against the wall to cry and did not, and looked at the poplars for a while, and that is the last thing I remember of that afternoon.
Here is the honest account of what happened, which I have never given anybody in full.
There was no transition.

That is the whole of it and it is why nobody in that place could ever explain it to anybody outside. I did not arrive anywhere. There was no going, no falling, no sensation of travelling, no moment. What happened is that at some point I noticed I was somewhere else and had been for a while — the way you notice you have been reading the same line four times, and you cannot say when you stopped.
I was standing in a garden.
I need to describe it exactly, because it was described back to me by two hundred people over the following ten years and I need it on the record that this is what I saw first.
It was dry. That is the first thing. Bare packed earth the colour of pale clay, swept smooth, hard underfoot. Nothing was growing in it.
There was a wall all the way round. Mud brick, tea-coloured, weathered, higher than a man, unbroken.
There was no gate. Not a closed gate. No gate anywhere in it, in any direction, and I walked a long way along that wall and there was no break in it at all.

Down the exact centre of the garden ran a watercourse in a stone channel — narrow, straight, running from the near end to the far end, its stone lips worn smooth and rounded the way ours were, though I had not yet done half of ours. The water in it was shallow and completely still and held a flat grey reflection of a sky that had nothing in it.

I did not cross it. I want to be precise about this because everybody asks and everybody wants it to be a prohibition. It was not. Nobody stopped me. There was no fear and no warning and no barrier. I simply did not want to and it did not occur to me to want to, in the way it does not occur to you to walk into someone else’s house because their door is open.

And at the far end, small with distance, there was one low tree with fruit on it. A pomegranate. The fruit was dark and there were perhaps six of them and it was the only living thing in that place and the only colour.

I did not get closer to it. I walked toward it for what felt like a considerable time and it stayed exactly the same distance away, and I was not frightened by that either, and I have never been able to explain why not.

There was no pain in that garden and there was no comfort. No heat and no cold. I could not smell anything at all — not the earth, not the water, and that is the detail everybody seizes on afterwards and finds funny, and it is the detail that convinces me, because I would never have invented it. The light was the flat white glare of one in the afternoon with no sun anywhere in the sky. There was no sound except, once or twice, water.
And there was somebody behind me.
At about the height of a hand on a shoulder. Slightly to the left. Not touching, exactly — or touching in the way you know a hand is on you when you have your coat on.

He had been there the whole time. That is the thing I understood without being told. Not: someone has come up behind me. But: this is where he stands, and he has been standing there since before I noticed anything, and he will be standing there afterwards.
I did not turn round.

I want to be very careful here because I have had twenty years to make this sound better than it was. I did not turn round because I was frightened. That is not true and I will not write it. I did not turn round because I did not want it to stop.

I understood, in some way I cannot defend, that turning round was a thing that would end the afternoon, and that I had nowhere else to be, and that eleven people were in the ground behind the kitchen.
So I stayed where I was, near the wall, on the right-hand side, and looked at the water.

Golnaz found me at about six in the evening. I had been out there since one. My hands were cold enough that she made a fuss about them and I could not answer her sensibly for about a quarter of an hour.
She asked me where I had been.
And I said: ‘Nowhere. I was sitting.’
Which was true, and was the first lie I told in that place, and I did not understand until much later that they are the same sentence.
THE FOURTH NIGHT
I gave it away, God.
I had it for eleven days and I gave it to a dying woman
because she was frightened and I had nothing else in my hands,
and I want it recorded that I meant well,
because I can see from here
that this is going to be the last time in this account
that meaning well is going to be enough.
I told the first person on the twenty-ninth of March, 1943.

Her name was Robab — the second Robab, the young one, twenty-four, who had come to us at fifteen and who had a bad winter and did not recover from it. She was not dying of the disease. Nobody in that place has ever died of the disease. She had a chest thing left over from February and she was not strong enough to put it down.

She was frightened. That is all. She was twenty-four and she was frightened at night and there was nobody to sit with her because her mother was in the ground behind the kitchen since the twelfth of February.
I sat with her for four nights.

And on the fourth night she asked me what happens, and I did not have an answer, and Amanollah had said the words to her twice that week and she had listened politely and had asked me anyway, which tells you what she thought of the words.
So I told her about the garden.

I told her the whole of it. The dry ground, the wall with no gate, the water down the middle, the tree at the far end that stays the same distance. I did not tell her about the hand. I have gone over that decision for twenty years and I still do not know whether it was mercy or cowardice and I have stopped expecting to find out.
And she said: ‘How do I get there?’
And I said the sentence that I have had to live with.
I said: ‘Sit down and let it get boring, and go through the boring, and do not come back out.’

That is all it is. That is the entire instruction and it has never needed another word in twenty years. You sit. Nothing happens. It becomes boring in a specific and quite unpleasant way — an itching, wanting, restless boredom, which for them is not physical because nothing in them itches, and is therefore purely a boredom of the mind. And you go through it, the way you walk through a doorway you cannot see, and you do not turn back, and at some point you notice you are already somewhere else and have been for a while.
Robab did it on the second afternoon.
I was there. I was sitting beside her bed with some mending because I could not do it myself and never have and never will.
She was gone for about forty minutes. I could see her breathing and her eyes were open and she did not move at all, and I sat there with my mending and got very frightened and did not call anybody.
And when she came back she cried for a long time and would not say why, and then she said:
‘It is dry.’
I said yes.
She said: ‘There is nothing growing.’
I said no.
And she said: ‘I do not know why that is the best thing anybody has ever given me.’
She died eleven days later. In those eleven days she went four times and told her aunt, who told nobody, and told a boy called Ali who was thirteen and who did not manage it for a year.

She was not frightened at the end. I want that in these pages because it is the only clean thing in this chapter. She was twenty-four and she was not frightened, and I did that, and I would do it again this afternoon, and everything that follows is also true.
TEACHING GOLNAZ
I have taught it like a recipe, God.
Sit. Let it get boring. Go through the boring.
Three sentences and a hand on the arm,
the way you would teach somebody bread.
Is that what You did?
Is that all it ever was —
somebody telling somebody else where to stand?
Golnaz was twenty-four in 1943 and she had been in that place thirteen years and her mother had died in February and she had not cried once.
I taught her in June.

I did not sit her down and instruct her. I told her because we were washing sheets and because she asked me, straight out, what I had been doing with Robab in that room, and because I have never been able to lie to Golnaz and have never tried more than once.
She listened to the whole thing with her hands in the water and did not interrupt.
Then she said: ‘Homa. Why did you not tell me first?’

I have never been forgiven for that, incidentally. Not in nineteen years. She has never mentioned it again and she has never forgotten it either, and every so often, in a particular kind of argument, it is in the room with us.
She went the same week. She has never told me what it was like the first time and I have never asked, and this is one of perhaps four subjects on which we have an arrangement.
What I can report is what she did next, which is the whole of the reason this became what it became.
Golnaz taught it to nine people in eleven weeks.

She did it the way she does everything, which is briskly and in the kitchen. She did not treat it as a revelation and she did not treat it as a comfort. She treated it as a skill — as something the House had turned out to possess, like a way of proving dough or a knack for a particular knot, and which it would be stupid not to pass on.

And that is why it spread. Not because it was holy. Because Golnaz Sadeghi told eleven people in a kitchen that there was a thing you could do in the afternoon and that it was not difficult, and because in that place, if Golnaz says a thing is not difficult, it is not difficult.
By the autumn there were perhaps thirty.
By the spring of 1944 I had stopped being able to count.
And here is what I did not anticipate, and what nobody could have anticipated, and what I have never been able to make anybody outside that wall understand.
I taught it to people who could not feel their bodies.

I cannot do it. I have tried perhaps four hundred times in twenty years. I sit down and let it get boring and I go through the boring and at eleven minutes my hand goes to my face, and at nineteen minutes I get up.

I have been in that garden once, on the eighteenth of March 1943, in the worst week of my life, when I had not slept in six weeks and had washed four bodies and was, I now think, closer to being nobody than I have ever been before or since.
Once. In twenty-four years.
The people I taught it to go every single afternoon and think nothing of it.

They cannot be interrupted, and I can, and that is the entire difference between us, and it is the reason this account is being written by the one person in that House who has no idea what she is talking about.
FARIDEH
Here it is, God.
I said I would write it down when I had described them properly
and I have described them properly
and I have run out of things to describe.
I did it in April of 1936.
It took me eleven minutes and a sheet of school paper
and I signed it,
and I was proud of it,
and that is the part I would like You to hold on to.
I have been putting this off for a hundred pages and Robab’s aunt asked me a question in the spring of 1944 that made it impossible to go on putting off.
She asked me why I stayed.

Not why I came. Everybody asks why I came and I have a good answer for that. She asked why I stayed, in the sixth year, when I was not ill and never would be, and could have walked up that track any morning of any of those years and got a post in any town in the province with two years of state service and a clean record.
I said something about the children.
And she said, kindly, because she is a kind woman: ‘Khanum, you have not taught a class since the winter.’
So. April of 1936.

I was twenty-four and I taught at a girls’ school in Tabriz and the decree had come down in January. The chador was banned. Not discouraged — banned, in the street, enforced by police, and I have to describe what that actually looked like because people who were not there have decided it was a liberation and people who were there have decided it was a persecution and it was both, in the same street, on the same afternoon, to different women.
I saw a woman of about fifty have her covering pulled off her head by a constable outside the bazaar and stand in the road holding her hands over her face and scream in a way I have not heard since.

I also stood in a classroom in front of forty girls with my head uncovered, in public, paid by the state, teaching them to read, which my grandmother — who was alive, and who came once and sat at the back and cried — could not have done in any year of her life.
Both. On the same afternoon. In the same street.
And I had decided which one mattered.

There was a woman on the staff called Farideh [fa-ree-DEH]. She was perhaps forty. She taught the younger ones and she was good at it and she was religious in the ordinary way of a woman of that generation, which is to say she prayed and she covered and she did not think about it any more than I thought about my shoes.
She had two daughters. Fourteen and eleven.
And when the decree came, she kept them home.

She did not protest. She did not make a speech. She simply did not send her daughters out of the house uncovered, and she came to work herself with her head bare and her jaw set like a woman going into cold water, and she cried about it in the store room where she thought nobody could hear, and she kept her girls at home for eleven weeks.
And I reported her.
