I want to be exact about the mechanism because the mechanism is the whole of my guilt.

It was not an anonymous denunciation. I did not slip a note under a door. I wrote to the district education office, on school paper, in my own hand, and I set out the position clearly and reasonably: that a member of the teaching staff was withholding her own children from education in defiance of the law and that this was an unsuitable example in a school for girls.
I signed it. I put my name and my position at the bottom and I read it over once and I was satisfied with it.

I was proud of it. That is the sentence I have been walking around for eight years to avoid writing. I was not frightened into it and I was not ordered to do it and nobody was watching me. I did it because I believed it, and I believed it because I had been given a school and a salary and a place in a modern country, and because the language was available to me — backward, the old thinking, she will thank us — and because I was twenty-four and had never in my life been on the receiving end of anything.
She lost her post in June.
Her husband was taken and questioned. I was told for two days and I have never known more than that, and I have never established what was done to him or by whom or for how long, and he was released.
And eighteen months later I was told something about the elder daughter.

I was told it second-hand, in a corridor, by a woman who was not certain and who was passing it on as gossip. I have never been able to verify it. I made two attempts, in 1937 and in 1939, and got nothing either time, and I am not going to write down what I was told, because I do not know that it is true and because the girl is a real person who is now a woman of about forty somewhere in this country and none of this is hers to carry.

I will write only this. What I was told was the kind of thing that happens to a fourteen-year-old girl who has been taken out of a school and put in a house for a year and whose father has been questioned and whose family has no money.
I left Tabriz eleven months later.

I came here because it was the furthest thing from an education office that I could find and because nobody here had heard of me and because a man in an office said nobody understands until they are in it and I thought he meant the disease.
And I stayed. Six years by then, and eighteen more after that.
Because I had already once been part of a project that was certain it was curing people, and had used its language, and had signed my name, and had been proud.
WHAT GREW INSTEAD
They are describing my garden back to me, God,
in the kitchen, at the ovens, in the yard,
people I have never spoken to,
and they are getting the details right,
including two I have never said out loud to anybody.
I would like to know what I have done.
I would like to know whether I found a door
or built a room.
It stopped being mine in the winter of 1944 and I can give the exact conversation.

A woman called Nosrat, who had come to us in 1942 and who I had spoken to perhaps six times in two years, was queueing at the ovens and said to the woman in front of her, about nothing, in the tone you would use about a shortcut into town:
‘I have never been down the far end. Have you?’
And the other woman said no, and that her husband had, and that there was nothing there anyway.
I stood behind them with a basin and did not move.
Over the following eight months I did what I do, which is that I counted and I recorded and I checked, and I have the pages still and I am not going to reproduce them here.

I asked forty-one people, separately, never two in the same room, never repeating back what the last one had said, never using a leading word. I asked them one question: when you sit in the afternoon, where do you go?
Forty-one described a walled garden.

Thirty-eight volunteered the watercourse without being asked. Thirty-one volunteered the pomegranate. The rest said only that there was something at the far end and that they had never got close enough to see it.
Nine of them told me that they could not smell anything there and every single one of the nine thought this was funny.
Twenty-six placed themselves in it. Near the wall. On the left, by the water. At the shaded end, though there is no shade.
And fourteen of the twenty-six placed *other people* in it.

That is the thing. That is the thing I have never got past and never will. A man of fifty told me, without any drama, in a doorway, that Nosrat stands near the wall on the left and does not come past the water. I checked it with Nosrat four days later. He was right. He had never spoken to her about it. I asked him how he knew and he looked at me as though I had asked how he knew where the kitchen was, and said: ‘Because that is where she stands.’
I checked eleven of them. Eleven of eleven agreed.
And here is where I have to stop and be honest with You and with whoever reads this, because I have carried both of these for twenty years and I have never once been able to choose between them.
Either there is a place, and it was always there, and a hundred people found the door to it because their bodies stopped shouting long enough for them to hear something the rest of us cannot.

Or I described a garden to a dying woman in March of 1943, and she described it to two people, and Golnaz described it to nine, and within eighteen months a hundred people were describing my garden back to me in a kitchen queue — and they were all standing in a room I built, in furniture I chose, and none of them will ever know, and I am the only person in the world who could tell them, and I have not.
The word for what stands behind them is mine as well.

They asked me, in that first year, what to call it. I said mehmān [meh-MAAN] — the guest, the one who is received — and I said it as a joke, in the House’s own register, because the joke is that you set a place for a guest and you feed him and you do not ask him when he is leaving.
Everybody laughed.
It is now what he is called. It is what the children call him. It has been what he is called for nineteen years and nobody remembers that it was a joke and nobody remembers who made it.
THE TRADE
They are not pitiable, God.
I have been here six years and I came here full of pity
and it has all been used up
and what is underneath it is something I did not order.
They can do a thing I cannot do.
They paid for it with their hands and their eyes.
And I am not sure — I am asking honestly —
I am not sure it was a bad trade,
and that is the sentence I would like You to argue with.
Ozra put it to me in the school in the autumn of 1944 and she did not put it as an argument. She was ruling a page.
I had said something — I do not remember what, something with pity in it, something about how much they had lost — and she let me finish, and then she said:
‘What do you believe in, Khanum?’
I said I did not understand the question.
‘You were a teacher in a city. You believed in something. Everybody who comes here believed in something in a city.’ She went on ruling. ‘Tell me one of them.’

I said, because it was the first thing to hand and because I had been thinking about Farideh: that a person should look at what is actually in front of them. That the worst thing you can do is turn your face away from something because it is unpleasant. That this is more or less the whole of morality.
Ozra said: ‘Good. Now do it.’
I said I did not follow.
‘Look at something unpleasant,’ she said. ‘Not for a moment. For an hour. Do not move and do not go and get a glass of water and do not think about the water. An hour. Can you?’
I said that nobody can do that.
‘We can,’ she said.
And then she put the pen down, which she almost never did, and gave me the thing that has been in my chest ever since.
She said: every one of those beliefs costs a nerve.

To look at what is in front of you, you must not flinch — and flinching is a nerve. To have a thought that is yours and finish it, you must not be interrupted — and interruption is a nerve. To sit with a dying woman all night and be of any use, you must be able to stay in the room, and the reason people leave the room is not cowardice, it is that the body makes them leave. To decide for yourself whether a thing is right, rather than accepting what you were handed, you need silence to think in, and out there nobody has had five consecutive minutes of silence in the whole of human history.

‘Your city believes in all of it,’ she said. ‘Every one of those is on a wall in a school somewhere in Tabriz. And not one person in that city can do any of it, because their bodies will not permit it, and so they admire it instead. Admiring a thing is what you do when you cannot do it.’
I said: ‘And you can.’

‘We do it every afternoon,’ she said, ‘between one and three, and nobody outside this wall has ever done it once, and we do not think it is remarkable, and we paid for it with everything you can see from this window.’

I want to be clear that she was not saying the disease is a blessing. She never said that, not once in twenty-four years, and I never heard anybody in that place say it either. Robab died at twenty-four. The boys were nine and eleven. Nobody there was grateful.
The claim was narrower and much worse.

The claim was that the outside world holds a set of beliefs it is physically incapable of practising, and that we had, by accident, by catastrophe, by the loss of the most ordinary thing a body does, become the only people on earth who could actually do them.
And that we knew it, and they did not.
That is why I stayed. Not the children. Not guilt, though there was plenty. Not because I could not go back — I could have gone back any morning of any of those years.

I stayed because I had spent my whole life believing in a way of being a person, and at the age of thirty-two I met sixty people who could do it, and I could not, and I never would, and the only thing left available to me was to stand near them.
PART FIVE — WHAT GREW
TWO ROOMS
She has taken the school, God,
and I have let her,
and I told myself it was because I am tired
and because she is better with them,
and both of those are true
and neither of them is the reason.
The reason is that she asked me for it
in a way that was not a question,
and I have never once in nine years
found the place to put my foot down.
Ozra took the school in the spring of 1944 and I gave it to her without a word being said about it.

I had been the teacher for six years. It was the post I was hired for. There were, by then, thirty-one children in that place and two rooms and a stack of primers that had come from the town in 1939 and had not been added to since, and I had taught in it every morning apart from the winter of 1943, when nobody taught anything.
And in March of 1944 Ozra said: ‘I will take the mornings.’

That was all. She did not ask. She did not offer to help. She said she would take the mornings and she took them, and I found myself saying yes and then found myself, over about four weeks, no longer going in, and at some point in May I understood that I had stopped being the teacher and that there had been no moment at which this was decided.

I want to be fair to her and to myself. She was better at it. That is simply true. I taught the way I had been taught in a training college in Tabriz, which is to say I stood at the front and I was pleasant and I got through the primer, and the children liked me and learned about as much as children usually learn.
Ozra taught standing up and never once opened a book in front of them.

She did arithmetic aloud, fast, at them, and would not let a wrong answer pass and would not humiliate anybody for one either, which I have never seen anybody else manage. She read to them from the Shahnameh in the afternoons — Rostam, Siyavash, the ones with the horses — and they were quiet for it in a way they were never quiet for me. She had them writing letters to nobody, as an exercise, and correcting each other’s.
And she did the other thing, which is the thing I want on this page.
She taught them to be looked at.

There is no version of this in any school in the world and there was no version of it in that place before her. She built it into the day, in the last quarter of an hour, and she called it nothing at all — it was simply what happened before they went home.

They paired off, small ones with bigger ones, and they went over each other. Feet first. Then shoes, turned over, a finger round the inside seam. Then hands, palm and back and the web between the fingers. Then forearms. Then faces.
And she stood at the front and talked them through it, every day, in a flat instructional voice, the way you would teach long division.
What are you looking for. Say it.
An opening.
Where do openings begin.
Where the shoe touches.
Show me where the shoe touches.
Thirty-one children, aged four to fourteen, learning the sequence by rote before they learned their times tables.

And I stood at the back of that room one morning in the summer of 1944 and watched a girl of six hold a boy of nine’s foot in her lap and turn it to the light and inspect the sole of it with complete seriousness, and I thought: they will do this every evening for the rest of their lives and they will never know that anybody had to decide it.
That is what a school is for. I had been running one for six years and I had thought it was for the primers.
ROQI’S HANDS
There is a wedding, God, and I have been crying since the drum
started
and nobody has noticed because everybody is crying,
and a girl of nineteen has just been carried round the yard on a chair
by four people with no fingers between them,
and I have never in my life
been anywhere less like a place where something is wrong.
They married in September of 1945 and it was the first wedding since before the war and the House lost its mind about it.
Roqi was nineteen and had come to us at seven. Habib was twenty-two and had been born in that bowl of ground in a house forty feet from where they were married.

I have been asked about the weddings more than anything else. Everybody who has ever heard about that place asks the same question with their face and not their mouth, and the question is: what were they celebrating?
So I am going to describe this one properly.
It took nine days to prepare and every single person had a job, and the jobs were assigned by Effat in the manner of a general who has been planning the campaign since spring, which she had.

They whitewashed everything. All of it, the whole compound, in three days, which we did twice a year anyway but never like that. They cleared the yard between the kitchen and the school and swept it and swept it again. The boys were sent to the hills for the wild rue and came back with far too much and were praised for it.
And the women did Roqi’s face.
I want to write about this because it is the thing I would put in front of anybody who thinks they know what that place was.

Four women did her, over about three hours, in the room behind the kitchen, and among the four of them there were perhaps eleven fingers that worked. Golnaz did the kohl because Golnaz’s hands were still good then and because Golnaz has an extremely steady hand and an extremely poor opinion of everybody else’s.
And a woman called Parvin, who had nothing at all left below the second knuckle on either hand and who had been doing brides in that village for eleven years, did the eyebrows.

She held the thread in her teeth and one loop over the stump of her left hand and worked it with her right wrist and her mouth, and she did it fast, and she did it perfectly, and Roqi sat there with her eyes shut and did not flinch once, and the room was extremely loud.

The talk in that room was the filthiest I have heard in my life. I am not going to reproduce any of it. There were six women in there and a girl of nineteen who was about to be married and the things that were said to her, kindly, by women of sixty, would not be printed in this country and possibly not in any other, and Roqi laughed until she had to be told to stop laughing because it was ruining her eyes.
Then they put her in red and took her out.

There was a tar and a reed and a drum, and the drum was played by a man called Mokhtar who had no fingers on either hand and who played with the flats of both palms and who was — and I have heard music in Tabriz and in Tehran and I am not being sentimental — the best musician I have ever been in a yard with.

They danced until the light went. An old woman of seventy-odd, who had nothing left of either hand and had not danced in years, was pulled into the circle by two girls and danced beautifully with her forearms held up, laughing, and the whole yard shouted.
And somebody asked Habib the question.

I had better explain it, because it is the worst joke in that place and I have only heard it asked twice in twenty-four years and both times were at weddings, which is the only place it is ever asked.

Nobody in that House has ever died of the disease. It does not kill you. It takes the warnings away and then it stands back and lets the ordinary world do the rest — a pan, a nail, a stove, a fall, an eye that stopped closing. Every grave behind that kitchen is somebody who was not told.
So they ask a man on his wedding day, in front of everybody, the way you ask a child what he wants to be:
Habib jan — what do you think will get you?
And Habib, who was twenty-two and had been born there and had heard it asked once before in his life, did not miss.
He said: ‘A woman.’
And put his hand out towards Roqi, and the yard came down.

I have thought about that for seventeen years. It is the funniest thing I have ever heard said in that place and it is also, and I want both of these in the same sentence, a boy of twenty-two being asked in public what he expects to be killed by and having a good answer ready because he has had one ready since he was fourteen.
Neither of them had a mark on them.
I noticed it at the time and I noted it and I did not think about it for another year, and it is in the next chapter and it is the worst thing in this book.
ASHRAF
A child has been born, God,
who has never seen the road,
and who will not see it,
and who will grow up believing that a wall is what a horizon is,
and I held her this afternoon
and thought about that
and could not make it come out as a bad thing,
and I have been trying since four o’clock.

The first child born inside the wall who never went out was a girl called Ashraf, and she was born in the November of 1945, and she is seventeen now and she is still there and she has never in her life been up that track.

There had been children born there before. Of course there had. But they had all come in from somewhere, or had gone out to the town for something at some point — a hospital, a relative, an errand — and had seen a road and a shop and other people.
Ashraf never did. There was no reason to take her out and it did not occur to anybody and she never asked.
She was two years old before she saw a stranger.

I taught her to read, incidentally. Ozra had the school by then but I did the small ones some afternoons when I could, and I taught Ashraf her letters in 1950 and she was quick and impatient and she is quick and impatient now.
And when she was about six she asked me what was on the other side of the wall.
I said: the rise, and then the track, and then the road, and then the town.
And she said: ‘What is a town?’
I explained a town. Shops, streets, a bazaar, thousands of people, a mosque with two minarets, a school with two hundred girls in it.
She listened to the whole thing and thought about it and then she asked the question I have never been able to answer.
She said: ‘Do they look at each other?’
I said: not like we do.
And she said: ‘Then who tells them?’
I said that they could feel it themselves. That their hands and their feet worked properly, and that if a stone got into a shoe out there they would know within one step and take the shoe off.
Ashraf considered this.
And then she laughed — a proper laugh, from a six-year-old, delighted — and said: ‘Every time?’
And I said yes. Every time.
And she said: ‘All day? Every little thing? That is horrible.’

I have never recovered from that conversation and I have never told anybody about it, and I am putting it here because it is the exact centre of everything I have to say and because a child of six got there in eleven seconds and it took me twelve years.

She was not being clever. She was six. She had simply never been given the assumption, and so when she was handed the facts she drew the obvious conclusion from them, which is that a body that reports every single thing that touches it, all day, without stopping, from the moment you wake until the moment you sleep, is a terrible way to have to live.
She was not wrong.

That is the thing. She was not wrong, and nobody has ever been able to tell me why she was wrong, and Ozra built a school around it, and I stood at the back of the room and watched it being built and helped.
WHERE HER MOTHER STOOD
I have found something out, God,
and I have checked it eleven ways
and I would like it not to be true.
It is not a comfort. Comforts do not do this.
Comforts do not run in families.
I am asking You directly and I will not ask again:
what have I opened,
and how long has it been open.
In the spring of 1946 I noticed something and spent four months proving it and have never told a living soul, and this is the first time it has been written down.
It began with Roqi.

She had married in September and by the spring she was going in the afternoons — she had learned it at fourteen, everybody learns it at fourteen now, Ozra sees to that — and I asked her, in the ordinary way, in the kitchen, where she stood.
She said: near the wall, on the left, and she has never been past the water.
And I said, without thinking, because I had been keeping the pages for three years and the pages were in my head: that is where your mother stands.
And Roqi said: ‘Yes.’
Not surprised. Not interested. In the tone of a woman being told that she has her mother’s chin.
I went and got the pages.

I had forty-one interviews from 1944 and I had added to them since, and I had, by then, positions for a hundred and six people, and I spent four months in the evenings doing what I have done my whole life, which is to rule a column and fill it in.
Here is what I found and I have the sheets and I will burn them before I die.
Of the thirty-one people in that House who had a parent also in that House and also in the garden, *twenty-nine stood where their parent stood.*

Not near. Not similarly. In the position. Left wall, right wall, the shaded end, by the water, the far corner. Mothers and daughters, fathers and sons, and — this is the one that took the ground out from under me — an aunt and a niece who had never lived in the same house and had not particularly liked each other.
Two did not match. One of them was a boy whose father had died before the boy could walk. I do not know what to do with that and I have never known.

I checked it eleven ways. I asked the children before I asked the parents. I asked people who had no idea their parent had ever been asked. I asked Ozra to ask four of them for me so that it was not my voice. Nobody knew what I was doing and nobody has ever known.
Twenty-nine of thirty-one.
I sat in the school after dark with the lamp and the sheets in front of me and I understood three things in about the space of a minute and I have not slept properly since.

The first is that this is not a comfort. A comfort is a thing a frightened mind makes, and a frightened mind makes what it needs, and what a frightened mind does not do is put you in your mother’s exact place beside a wall you have never seen.

The second is that it is not simply a story being passed down, because I checked for that too, and mothers do not tell their children where they stand. I asked eleven mothers. Not one of them had ever discussed it. It does not come up. You do not discuss where you stand in the garden any more than you discuss which side of the bed you sleep on.
And the third.
I stand near the wall on the right.

I have been in that place once, in March of 1943, for one afternoon, and I stood near the wall on the right, and my mother is buried in Tabriz and never sat still in her life and never heard of this place.
I am not sick. I have never been sick. I am the one person inside that wall with a body that reports to her faithfully every day like an honest servant.
And it let me in anyway. Once. When I was closer to being nobody than I have ever been.
I do not know what that means and I have not asked anybody and there is no one to ask. What I know is that I stopped, that spring, being a woman who was recording something.
WHAT WE HEARD
There is fighting on the road, God.
We can hear it in the evenings when the wind is right.
Two men came over the wall in the night
and we have put them in the bathhouse
and nobody has asked them anything.
I used to think that not asking was cowardice.
I have come to think it is the only skill we have
that the outside world cannot do at all.

In the winter of 1945 a government was declared in Tabriz that was not the government in Tehran, and for about a year the province I was born in was a separate country with a separate flag, and then in December of 1946 the army came back up the road and took it, and there were reprisals, and I am not going to write an account of that because I do not have one.
Here is what we had.
We had gunfire in the evenings, some weeks, when the wind was from the north. Not close. The way you hear a wedding two villages away and cannot tell what it is.
We had the road closed twice, once for nine days and once for a fortnight.

We had the consignment three weeks late in January of 1947 and then not late again, with no explanation and no apology, and the man who brought it was a different man and we never learned what had happened to the first one.
We had, in the second week of December 1946, two men in the bathhouse.
They came over the wall in the night, which anybody can do, and Bahman found them in the morning and did not raise his voice, and they were in there nine days.

They were perhaps twenty-five and thirty. They had no weapons by the time they got to us, and one of them had a wound in his side that Effat dressed and that healed badly, and they were terrified for the first two days and then they were not.
Nobody asked them anything.
I want to be very exact about this because it is the purest example I have of what that place actually was.

There was no meeting about the men in the bathhouse. Nobody voted. Nobody stood up and said that we would shelter them and nobody stood up and objected, and no one ever said out loud whether they thought the men were Democrats running from the army or army men who had run from their unit, which were the only two things they could have been and which were, in that December, the difference between two entirely opposite kinds of trouble.

Food went down twice a day. Effat did the dressing. A boy took them a blanket. Amanollah went in on the fourth day and sat with them for an hour and came out and said nothing whatever about it, then or ever.
And on the ninth day they went, in the dark, and we never found out.
The rule — and it is not a rule, it was never spoken, I am writing it down for the first time in twenty-four years — is this.
We do not ask the outside what it is.

Not from fear, though there was fear. Because the moment you ask a man which side he is on, you have taken a side, and this place is a bowl of ground eleven kilometres past the end of a road containing a hundred and six people who cannot run.

I have come to think it is the single most sophisticated thing that House ever did, and it was never designed, and nobody in it could have explained it to you, and it is the same instinct that told Effat to say twenty-two to a man with a clipboard in 1942.
They did not lie to that man to protect a secret.
They lied to him because being counted is the first step in being decided about.
SOHRAB
A child has gone out, God,
and he did not want to go
and we did not want him to go
and he went,
and there was nothing anybody could do,
and I want You to know that we did nothing wrong today
and it was still the worst thing that has happened here
since the winter,
and I am beginning to wonder
whether those two facts have ever been related.
They took Sohrab in the August of 1946 and it was entirely legal and entirely correct and nobody did anything wrong.

He was six. His mother had died in 1944 and his father was in the House and was ill in the way that the state notices, which is to say visibly, and there was a provision — there had always been a provision, it was not new, it was not aimed at us — that a child who was not himself infected should not be raised in a leprosarium.
Nineteen people out of twenty cannot catch this thing. Sohrab had been in that place since birth and had never had a mark on him and was, like most of the children there, simply one of the nineteen.

So a man came with a paper, and Sohrab’s father signed it because he could not not sign it, and a woman from a charitable institution in Tabriz came in a car with a driver and took a boy of six away to a dormitory with forty beds in it, and she was kind, and she cried on the way out, and she was doing her job and her job was correct.
I have no complaint to make about any of them. I want that in these pages, because it is the whole point and because everybody expects the other kind of story.
Nobody was cruel to Sohrab. He was fed and schooled and he is, so far as we know, alive and well and working somewhere in this country as a grown man of twenty-two.
He screamed in the yard.

That is what I have. That is what I carry from that August. A boy of six screaming in a yard, and a hundred people standing there, and his father sitting on the step with the paper still in his hand, and nobody able to do one single thing about it, and the woman from the institution saying, over and over, that he would settle, and being right.
Two things came out of that day and they have both been on my mind for sixteen years.
The first is that on the night before, Ozra took him into the school and sat with him for two hours, and I did not know what she was doing and did not ask.
I know now. She was making sure he could go.
Every child in that House learns it at fourteen and always has. He was six. She taught it to him in one evening because there was one evening.
And the second thing is the letter.

It came in 1949 — three years, no word, nothing, and then a letter written for him by somebody at the institution, in a hand that is not a child’s hand, with his name signed at the bottom in a child’s hand. Nine lines. He was well. He was learning a trade. He remembered the poplars. He hoped his father’s health was good, which it was not, and which nobody had told him.
And then, at the bottom, in the same borrowed handwriting, because he had dictated it to somebody who did not know what he was writing:
Tell Khanum Ozra that it is the same. Tell her I still do not go past the water.
He was nine years old and he was ninety kilometres away in a dormitory in Tabriz and he had been out of that House for three years.
Ozra read it standing up, in the yard, and folded it, and put it in her pocket, and said: ‘Good.’
And that is the day the House found out what it had.
PART SIX — THE BEGINNING OF THE COLD
SEASON
GOOD NEWS
This is the last time I am going to address You,
and I want to be fair, so I will say what I have and not what I feel.
A young man came today with a case
and everything in it was good.
Everything in it was what I asked You for
in the winter of 1943, out loud, in a kitchen, with my hands in a basin.
It has come.
It has come eleven years late and it has come to the wrong place
and I do not think that was Your doing.
I think there was simply nobody at the other end,
exactly as he said,
and I have been talking to a room.

Sarabi died in 1946 of a thing in his stomach and the man who replaced him was twenty-nine years old and his name was Dr Tahmasbi and he came for the first time in the March of 1947 in a coat that had been bought for him.
I liked him. I want that first. He was not a fool and he was not a careerist and he had asked for this district, which nobody asks for.

He did eleven examinations an hour, the way Sarabi had, and he was faster and more thorough and he wrote everything down, and at the end of the day he came and found me because I was the one who spoke like a person from a city and because he had something he wanted to say to somebody who would understand what it was.
He had a case with him.
He put it on the table in the school and he opened it and he was so pleased that he had to stop and start again.
He said: it works.
He said the name of it, which I did write down that time, and which I am not going to put in these pages because I do not want anybody reading this to think that this is a story about a drug.

He said it had been in use for six years in America and four in India. He said the results were not partial and were not a management of symptoms and were not a slowing. He said that people took it by mouth, over a period of years, and that the thing stopped, and that it stopped in nearly everybody, and that once it had stopped it did not come back.
He said the word cured, twice, and the second time he said it slowly because he could see I had not taken it.
I asked whether it repaired anything.

And he was honest, immediately, which is why I liked him. He said no. He said what is gone is gone — a dead nerve does not come back, a hand that has closed does not open, an eye that has clouded does not clear. He said: I cannot give anybody back a finger.
He said: but nobody here will lose another one.
I want to set down what I felt in that room because I have been accused of a great deal in my own head over the last fifteen years and this at least I can answer.

I was happy. Completely, stupidly, physically happy, in a way I had not been since before the war. I put both hands flat on that table and I laughed, and Tahmasbi laughed, and I said something like at last and he said yes, at last, and neither of us was performing.

I thought of Robab, who was twenty-four, and of the boys, and of Zohreh’s foot, and of every single grave behind that kitchen, all of which were, without exception, the graves of people who had been killed by not being told — and I understood that from this March onward nobody in that bowl of ground would ever be added to that ground for that reason again.
That is what was in the case.
I have had fifteen years to be honest about the next part and I am going to be.
Somewhere in the second hour, while he was still talking, while I was still glad, a small cold thing arrived at the back of my mind and sat down and did not say anything.
It had been sitting in me since the October of 1941 and a cigarette put out on a wall.
And I did not identify it, and I did not speak, and I went on being happy for the rest of that day.
WHAT IT WOULD MEAN
—

The first meeting was four days later and it was not a meeting either. It was eleven people in the school in the evening because that is who came, and it went on until after midnight, and there was nothing decided at all.

Tahmasbi had left the case. He was coming back in six weeks. He had left enough to begin nineteen people and had said, cheerfully, that within a year he expected to have enough for everybody and that we should start with the worst.

I want to set out what was in that room, as flatly as I can, because everything afterwards was decided by it and because I have read what the world writes about places like ours and the world thinks this decision was made by a monster in a locked room.
Here is what was in the room.

*Bahman spoke first*, because Bahman always speaks first when he does not understand something. He wanted to know what happened after. Not medically. He said: I am forty-three, I have this pair of hands, I am not going to get better hands. What am I doing in two years?
And Effat said: you are doing what you are doing now.
And Bahman said: no, Khanum, because in two years there is no reason for me to be here.
That was the whole thing. That is the entire argument and it was in the room in the first four minutes, spoken by a man who could not have constructed it on paper.
Because Bahman was correct.
I am going to lay it out the way it lay out that night.

A hundred and six people were in that bowl of ground for exactly one reason: the state and their families and the towns had decided they should be somewhere else. That is the only thing every person in that place had in common. It was the reason there was a consignment. It was the reason nobody came up that track. It was the reason we were left alone.

Cure them, and within a few years there is a hundred and six people, average age forty-four, with no land, no trade that anybody would hire, hands that could not do most work and faces that would not be served in a shop, no families that would have them back — a great many of whom had been given up for dead by relatives in the thirties — and no legal reason whatever to be receiving a monthly cart.

The cart stops. That is not cruelty. There is no entitlement for cured people. The whole apparatus, thin as it was, exists because of an illness, and when the illness goes, the apparatus goes, and the people do not.
*Golnaz said the second thing* and she said it standing up.
She said: I am not talking about the cart. I am talking about Ashraf.
Ashraf was two. Ashraf had never seen a road.

Golnaz said: there are thirty-one children in that school. Nineteen of them will never have this thing because they cannot get it. Every one of them stays here because their parents are here. Cure the parents and the parents are dispersed and the children go with them into a town, and what are they in a town? They are the children from the leper village. Every one of them, for the rest of their lives, in a place where everybody knows.
She said: in here they are children. Out there they are a story about somebody’s childhood.
*And then Amanollah asked the question that nobody had asked.*
He was fifty-three. He had been doing the rites for four years with nothing at the other end. He had said nothing for two hours.
He said: ‘How many will it save?’
Nobody understood him.
He said: ‘We have been talking about what we lose. I would like the other number. If we take it — all of us, tomorrow — how many people who would otherwise die will not die?’
And nobody could answer, because nobody knew, and Tahmasbi was not there.
So Ozra opened the exercise book.

She had, by then, nine years of it. Every arrival, every death, every cause, in that small upright hand that never varied. She did it there, at the table, in front of eleven people, with a pencil, and it took her about twenty minutes and nobody spoke while she did it.
And she said: about one a year. Perhaps one and a half.
Then she said the rest of it, because she is thorough and because she does not soften anything.

She said: but not from the disease. Nobody here dies of the disease. They die because they were not told — a foot, a stove, an eye that stopped closing. The drug stops the thing from taking any more warnings away. It does not give back the warnings that are already gone. Every person in this room who is already blind will still be blind, and every person whose hands have closed will still have closed hands, and every one of those people can still die of a stove.
She closed the book.

She said: ‘The Looking saves those. Not the drug. The drug saves the ones who have not lost it yet, which is the children, and the children are not the ones being offered it, because he said start with the worst.’
I have thought about that for fifteen years and I have never found the error in it and I have looked.
WHAT AMANOLLAH PROPOSED
—
It was the fourth meeting and it was the middle of May and it had been going nowhere for six weeks, and it was going nowhere because everybody in that room was decent and nobody would say the thing.
Amanollah said it.

I want to describe him as he was that night because everybody who reads this will want him to be someone else. He was fifty-three and he had been in that place nine years and he had buried, by my count, thirty-one people with his own hands, including eleven in five weeks in a winter when the ground was frozen. He had lost God in March of 1943 and had told one person and had gone on saying the words every single time anybody asked, for four years, at night, holding hands he could not feel, with nothing at the other end at all.
He was the kindest man I have known and I do not say that loosely and I am not saying it to soften what follows.
He said: ‘We should take it slowly.’
Somebody said that we did not have a choice about the speed, that Tahmasbi would bring what he brought.
And Amanollah said: ‘No. I mean we should ask him to bring less.’
There was a silence of some length.
He explained it patiently, the way he explained everything, and he had clearly been working on it for weeks and had not enjoyed any of it.

He said: if we take it fully, this place ends in five years. Not because anybody closes it. Because there is no reason for it, and the cart stops, and the young ones go first, and then it is thirty old people in a bowl of ground with no kitchen and no school and no one to look at their feet, and they die of stoves, one after another, and there is nobody to write it down.
He said: and if we do not take it at all, then we are choosing that children get this thing, and I will not do that and neither will anybody in this room.
He said: so there is a third thing.

And he laid it out. He had it exact. He had been to see Tahmasbi in the town, on his own, twice, and had asked him questions about doses in the manner of a man who was simply anxious about his people, and Tahmasbi had answered him fully because why would he not.

Amanollah said: it does not work at a fifth. At about a fifth of what he wants to give, it holds the thing in place. It does not clear it and it does not let it run. A person on that does not get worse quickly and does not get better at all. They live a long time. Thirty years, he thinks. They do not go blind fast. Their hands take twenty years instead of eight.
He said: and they remain, on any paper anybody looks at, ill.
I said — and I am the one who said it, and I am glad I said it and it changed nothing — ‘That is thirty years of it.’
And Amanollah said: ‘Yes.’
I said: ‘You are proposing that we keep it.’
And he said the sentence that I have carried since and that I have never repeated to anybody until this page.
He said: ‘I am proposing that we keep the reason they leave us alone.’
Then he sat down and put his hat on the table and said one more thing, and this is the part that nobody would believe of him and that I have to write because it is true.
He said: ‘I want it recorded that this is the worst thing I have ever thought of, and that I thought of it, and that nobody asked me to.’
THE VOTE
—
We voted on the eleventh of June, 1947, in the yard, after the evening Looking, because that was when everybody was already outside.
A hundred and six people. Everybody over fourteen, which was seventy-one.

There was no speech. Effat said what it was in about nine words, in the way that Effat says things, and there was no argument in the yard because six weeks of argument had already happened in the school and everybody knew where everybody stood.
They did it by hand, in the last of the light.
Fifty-eight for. Nine against. Four did not raise a hand at all and nobody made them.
I voted for it.
I am going to explain why, and I am not going to explain it in a way that makes it acceptable, because it is not acceptable and I have known that from the moment my arm went up.
I did not vote for it because I was persuaded by Amanollah’s arithmetic, although his arithmetic was correct.
I did not vote for it because of Bahman’s hands or the cart or the children in Ozra’s school, although all of that was true and all of it would have happened.
I voted for it because of April 1936.

Because eleven years before that evening I had sat in a staff room in Tabriz and decided that a woman called Farideh was going to be cured of her backwardness whether she liked it or not, and I had signed my name to it, and I had been proud, and a man in an office had been perfectly kind about it, and a girl of fourteen had been taken out of a school and put in a house.

And here was another cure, arriving from outside, in a case, carried by a good young man in a coat that had been bought for him, who was entirely certain and entirely well-meaning and entirely correct about the medicine.
And I was going to be asked, again, whether the people it was being done to should have any say in it.
I raised my hand.

I want to be very clear that this is not a defence. I have set it out honestly and I can see what it is. What I did in that yard was let a hundred and six people go on being ill for thirty years, in order to settle an account with myself from eleven years earlier, in a city, about a woman I never apologised to.
Amanollah did not raise his hand.

He proposed it, and he argued for it for six weeks, and he did not vote. He stood at the edge of the yard with his hands at his sides and let it happen and did not participate in it, and when I asked him about it afterwards, he said: ‘I am not going to be one of the ones who chose. Somebody has to be able to say afterwards that he did not choose.’
I said: ‘That is a distinction without much practical consequence.’
Which is what I had said to Ozra about the exercise book, in 1938, in my second week, and I heard myself say it and I heard it land.
Amanollah smiled at me. He was not offended. He was the least offendable man I have met.
He said: ‘Khanum, it is the only thing I have left.’

He died in the spring of 1953. He did the rites for a hundred and forty-one people in fifteen years and he never once said that anything came back, and by the end there were two boys he had trained who could do it as well as he could, and one of them does it now.

The arrangement with Tahmasbi took about a year to settle and I am not going to describe how it was done, because it does not matter and because the mechanism is dull and administrative and was mostly a matter of a quantity being requested in a letter and never being questioned by anybody at the other end, for twenty-two years, by four different men, none of whom ever came to look.
Nobody at the other end. That was Amanollah’s whole discovery, in the end, and it applied to more than one thing.
THE COLD SEASON
I am not writing to You any more.
I did it for nine years and it was a habit and it was company
and I have stopped, and I want to be accurate about why.
It is not that I decided You were not there.
It is that I noticed I had been writing to the House the entire time —
to this ground, these people, this wall we made out of the ground —
and that it had been answering me every single day
in the plainest possible language,
and that I had been so busy addressing the ceiling
that it took me nine years to look down.
So. To the House.
You have my whole life. You are welcome to it.
I would like to say that you did not ask for it,
but you did, in the winter of 1943, in a kitchen, in four words,
and I have never once been able to put it down.
Golnaz asked me, in the autumn of 1947, why I had voted the way I did.
We were doing the sheets, which is where everything in my life has been said.
I told her the truth. All of it — Farideh, the letter, the school paper, the eighteen months, the corridor. It took about twenty minutes and she did not interrupt once and her hands did not stop.
At the end she said: ‘So you voted about a woman in Tabriz.’
I said yes.
She said: ‘Homa.’ She almost never uses it. In nineteen years I could count it.
I said: ‘Yes. About a woman in Tabriz.’

And Golnaz said: ‘Khanum. You have been here nine years. There are three hundred people in this country who could have voted about a woman in Tabriz. Not one of them would have voted the way you did, because not one of them would have thought there was anything to vote about.’
I said that was not the point.

And she said: ‘It is exactly the point. You did the right thing for a reason that is nothing to do with us, and it is still the right thing, and you are going to sit in that basin for the rest of your life anyway.’ She wrung out a sheet. ‘Do you know what your problem is? You want to have done it for the correct reason. Nobody here has ever done anything for the correct reason. We do the thing and then we work out why afterwards and mostly we are wrong about that too.’
I said: ‘And that does not trouble you?’

And Golnaz Sadeghi, who was twenty-eight years old, who had buried her mother in a frozen February, who had taught nine people how to leave their own afternoons, and who has one working hand now and still does the kohl at every wedding in that House, said:
‘No. Because the sheets get clean either way.’

Tahmasbi came back in the November with the reduced quantity and did not query it and never queried it in the four years he had the district, and I do not know to this day whether he understood. I have decided that he did not. I have decided it in the way you decide a thing you would rather not test.

And that winter, in the January of 1948, a man from the ministry came up the track — the second and last outsider to come to us with a clipboard in twenty-four years — to ask why the requisition had changed and to satisfy himself that the arrangement was in order.
He talked to Ozra for about an hour in the school and drank three glasses of tea and went away satisfied.
I asked her afterwards what she had told him.
And she said: ‘I told him we are in the cold season.’
I said: ‘What does that mean?’
Ozra put the pen down, which she almost never did.

‘It means it is winter here,’ she said, ‘and it is going to be winter here, and we know it, and we are not asking anybody to make it spring. He wrote it in his book. He thought it was a country expression and he was charmed by it and now he can go home.’
She picked the pen back up.

‘It is not an expression,’ she said. ‘It is the most accurate sentence anybody has ever said about this place, and I will go on saying it to every one of them who ever comes up that track, and not one of them will ever ask me what I mean.’
Nobody ever did.
WHENEVER YOU ARE READY
—
I am fifty years old and it is the spring of 1962 and there is a young woman from Tehran in my house.

She has been here four days. She came up that track in a hired Jeep with a cameraman and a permit, and she has a face like somebody who has decided in advance not to flinch and is finding it harder than she expected, and I have watched two hundred people spend four days being extremely careful with her.

I do not know what will come of it. Ozra has views. Ozra has had views for six weeks and has been in the school with the door shut and I have not asked her, because I have got very good at not asking, and because I am fifty and have discovered that the last freedom available to a woman my age is the freedom to be told things later.
I have not been in the garden since 1943 and I do not expect to go again.

I still cannot sit still. I have tried perhaps four hundred times in twenty-four years and I get to eleven minutes and my hand goes to my face and at nineteen minutes I get up and go and find something to do. I am the only person over fourteen inside this wall who cannot do it. The children know. They are kind about it in the way that children are kind, which is to say not at all, and there is a whole thing they do that I am not going to describe.

Effat died in 1955. Bahman is alive and is fifty-eight and has one eye and his nail is in the tin. Golnaz has one working hand and does the kohl. Roqi has three children and the eldest stands where her mother stands, near the wall, on the left, and has never gone past the water.
Ashraf is seventeen and has never seen a road.
She is going to. That is a separate matter and it is coming and I know it is coming.
They want to film in here this morning. The young woman has asked, very politely, twice, and the second time she did not push, which I noticed and which is the reason I have said yes.
She wants me at the shelf.

There is a small mirror on it with flowers painted round the frame, propped against the wall, and beside it the teapot that has been on that shelf since before the wall, which came from my mother’s house in Tabriz in a bag in 1938 and is the only thing I brought.
She has asked me to do what I do in the mornings, which is to stand there and put my scarf right.
I said that this was not very interesting and she said that it was, and I have been doing this long enough to know when I am being handled, and I have decided to allow it.
So I am going to put down this pen, and go and stand in front of that mirror, and look at my own face, which is the one face inside this wall that nothing has ever happened to.
And she is going to say whenever you are ready.
And I am going to be ready, because I have been ready since 1938, and because there has never once been anybody there to say it to me.
GLOSSARY

Akhound [aa-KHOOND] · Persian — A Muslim cleric; a member of the religious class. Under Reza Shah the clergy were stripped of the courts, of control over religious endowments, and even of the licensed right to wear clerical dress without documentation.
Amanollah [a-maan-ol-LAAH] · Arabic, via Persian — Literally the security or protection of God. The Sheikh who came to bury one woman in 1938 and stayed nine years.
Ashraf [ash-RAF] · Arabic, via Persian — Most noble. The first child born inside the wall who never went out.
Azeri [a-ZEH-ree] · Turkic — The Turkic language spoken across north-western Iran, including the region around the House. Distinct from
Persian and not mutually intelligible with it.
Bahman [bah-MAN] · Persian, from Avestan Vohu Manah — Good mind or good purpose; also the eleventh month of the Iranian calendar. A roofer, and the holder of the House record.
Chador [chaa-DOR] · Persian — Literally a tent. The full outer covering worn by women, banned by decree in 1936 and enforced in the street by police.

Chahārbāgh [chaa-haar-BAAGH] · Persian — Literally four gardens. The classical Persian walled garden: four quarters divided by watercourses, enclosed against the desert. The oldest surviving image of paradise in the language — the English word paradise descends from an Old Persian term meaning a walled enclosure.
Che khabar [che kha-BAR] · Persian — Literally what news. An entirely ordinary greeting. Inside the House it is also a status report: whether any part of the body has troubled itself to send word.
Effat [ef-FAT] · Arabic, via Persian — Chastity, modesty. The woman whose sentences are four words long and end discussions before they start.
Farideh [fa-ree-DEH] · Persian — Unique, precious. A teacher in Tabriz who kept her daughters home in 1936.
Golnaz [gol-NAAZ] · Persian — Literally flower-grace. Nineteen in 1938; still doing the kohl at every wedding in 1962.
Habib [ha-BEEB] · Arabic, via Persian — Beloved. Born inside the wall; married in the yard in 1945.
Hich khabari nist [HEECH kha-ba-REE NEEST] · Persian — There is no news. The standard reply to che khabar, and in the House a report that nothing has been felt.
Homa [ho-MAA] · Persian — The mythical bird of Persian legend, said never to land. The narrator.

Khāmūshī [khaa-moo-SHEE] · Persian — Silence; quietness; the state of being extinguished. The name given in the House to the condition entered in the flat hour of the afternoon, and to the practice that produces it.
Khāneh [KHAA-neh] · Persian — House, home, dwelling. What the residents called the place. The state, on the one card that recorded it, called it a station.
Khanum [KHAA-noom] · Persian — Lady, madam. A term of respect used before or after a woman's name, or on its own.
Kohl [KOL] · Arabic, via Persian — Dark powder applied along the eyelid, used across the region for many centuries by women and men alike.

Mehmān [meh-MAAN] · Persian — Guest; visitor; one who is received. The name given in the House to the presence that stands behind a person in the garden, coined as a joke — you set a place for a guest, and you do not ask him when he is leaving.
Mokhtar [mokh-TAAR] · Arabic, via Persian — The chosen one. The drummer at the wedding, who played with the flats of both hands.
Negāh [ne-GAAH] · Persian — A look; a glance; the act of looking at. The

House's evening inspection, performed in pairs at the bell, in which each person's feet, shoes, hands, forearms and face are examined by another, because their own bodies will not report injury to them.
Nowruz [no-ROOZ] · Persian — Literally new day. The Iranian new year, falling at the spring equinox; the oldest continuously observed festival in the country.
Ozra [OZ-raa] · Arabic, via Persian — Virgin, maiden. Twenty-six on arrival, already ill, already writing things down.
Qur'an [kor-AAN] · Arabic — The scripture of Islam.
Roqi [ro-GHEE] · Persian, diminutive — Familiar form of Roghayyeh. Nineteen at her wedding in 1945.
Sakineh [sa-kee-NEH] · Arabic, via Persian — Tranquillity; the calm that descends. The woman who poured the tea.
Shahnameh [shaah-naa-MEH] · Persian — The Book of Kings, completed by
Ferdowsi around 1010, the national epic of Iran and the longest poem ever written by a single author. Read aloud in the school in the afternoons.
Sohrab [soh-RAAB] · Persian — A hero of the Shahnameh, killed in single combat by his own father, who does not recognise him until it is too late.
The first child taken out of the House.
Tar [TAAR] · Persian — A long-necked, waisted, plucked string instrument played across Iran and the Caucasus.
Zohreh [zoh-REH] · Persian — Venus, the planet. The woman whose foot changed how everybody in that place lived for twenty-three years.
